chapters.title: Growing Your Habits from Tiny to Transformative
Untangling Bad Habits: A Systematic Solution
The Elements of Behavior
chapters.hook: 3 minutes felt too small to change anything. I thought that until a skipped habit told on me.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the way failure feels, a missed habit usually points to a missing design piece. At the action moment, Motivation, Ability, and Prompt did not arrive together.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to skip a tiny action, set a 10-minute timer, walk, and choose which MAP piece to fix.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit fails, do not call yourself lazy. Replay that moment through B=MAP: was Motivation low, Ability too hard, or the Prompt missing?

breakdown.fastRead:
Pascal is halfway down the hall when he feels the old pull to keep walking. The pill case is still on the sink. He did care. He did decide. Yet the dose almost slipped, and by lunch his mind would have carried one more open loop.

Behavior happens in a moment. Motivation, Ability, and Prompt have to meet at that moment, or the action does not happen. Blame hides the missing part. A skipped habit is a design clue.

Replay the miss like a small film. Did you want it enough right then? Was the action easy enough? Did anything tell you to start? Fix the part that was absent.
breakdown.deepRead:
A formula helps only if it changes where you look. B=MAP is the simplest form of the Fogg Behavior Model: behavior happens when three parts meet. In plain words, you need enough want, an action you can do, and a cue that says now.

That lens is useful because it is fast. The Fogg Behavior Model is cited by over 1,900 academic publications, and the public model page ties it to the Stanford Behavior Design Lab. Those numbers will not brush your teeth for you. You need them to trust that this is not a pep phrase. It is a way to inspect one missed action without making your whole self the suspect.

Madeline sees this during a Behavior Design training case. The senior coaches keep asking why a group did not sign up. The new observer notices the prompt was buried under a long form. Motivation may have been fine. Ability may have been fair. The cue was nearly invisible.

A prompt is not persuasion. It is the thing that tells a ready person to start. A hard action can still happen when motivation is high. A low-motivation action must be very easy. So the first repair is not always more desire. Sometimes it is a smaller step or a better placed cue. The right diagnosis saves effort.
breakdown.fullRead:
The harder case arrives when you already know the model and still want to scold yourself. Cedric has the words on the page: Behavior, Motivation, Ability, Prompt. He also has a gym bag by the door and a rent notice on his phone. The bag has not moved all week, and the phone keeps winning.

B=MAP does not excuse the miss. It gives you a cleaner target. If Motivation is low, make the behavior smaller or connect it to something you already care about. If Ability is low, shrink the action until it fits the real day. If the Prompt is missing, put the cue where the behavior can start.

The model's edge is timing. You diagnose the action moment, not your whole life. A person can be caring and still miss a dose. A person can be organized and still forget a bill. The question is what was present when the behavior needed to happen.

The free 5-day practice makes the same point in miniature. It asks for 3 super easy habits for 5 days, with about 3 minutes of daily work. That small frame keeps Ability high. It also teaches a quiet lesson: you do not need a large mood to begin a small act.

The longer record keeps the lesson from feeling flimsy. The method draws on 20 years of research and a coaching base of over 60,000 people. Those numbers do not make your habit happen. They tell you where to look when your plan fails on an ordinary Tuesday.

Look at the four parts of B=MAP in order: Behavior, Motivation, Ability, Prompt. Behavior is the act you want, not a mood. Motivation is how much you want it right then. Ability is how easy it feels. Prompt is the cue that says start now. If you blur those parts, you fix the wrong thing. A bigger promise may feel noble. It may still leave breakfast without a cue.

Still, the model costs you something. It takes away the easy drama of being the problem. Gwen learns that during a short walk after dinner. She wants the old story: I never follow through. The timer is running, and she has to trade that story for a duller question. Which part of MAP failed?

The answer is not glamorous. Her evening stretch had no clear cue. She adds it after brushing her teeth and cuts the stretch to a few breaths. She gives up the stern speech, and she also gives up the rush of feeling doomed.

The trade is plain. Behavior Design asks you to stop using shame as proof that you care. You get a smaller next step. You lose the grand self-accusation. For many habits, that is a fair price.

examples.title: The Missing Prompt Memo
examples.scenario: "Stop asking who forgot," Pascal writes at the top of a one-page lab memo. In the Stanford Behavior Design Lab review queue, he marks the failed signup beside B=MAP: Motivation is present, Ability is fair, Prompt is missing. The older reviewers keep reading the lapse as weak follow-through. Pascal's memo points to the Fogg Behavior Model cited by over 1,900 academic publications and asks for a better cue.
examples.whatToDo: Pascal leaves the memo in decision form: keep the signup goal, shorten the first screen, and move the cue to the place where the user is ready to act.
examples.whyItMatters: The outsider sees what the practiced reviewers stopped seeing. B=MAP keeps the repair local: fix the prompt before giving people another lecture.

examples.title: Two Signups Diverge
examples.scenario: The signup cursor blinks while Bonnie reads the 5-day practice note: since 2011, participants have chosen 3 super easy habits for about 3 minutes a day. She picks actions she can do while tired. Across the booth, Madeline turns the same form into a full morning reset. Bonnie is ready to start after the receipt prints. Madeline is already sorting, renaming, and losing the thread.
examples.whatToDo: Bonnie keeps the practice tiny and names the first move before closing the form. Madeline needs to cut her plan until the start is as easy as the program asks.
examples.whyItMatters: The same prompt can produce two loads. A short practice protects Ability only when the person refuses to smuggle in a large hidden task.

examples.title: The New Coach's Case
examples.scenario: The senior coach's slot opens during a Behavior Design practice call, and Romain gets the learner case before his notes are ready. He starts to say the learner lacks drive. Aspen stops him from the edge of the group: "A missed prompt is a design clue, not a confession." The coaching base reaches over 60,000 people and 20 years of research. This repair begins with a smaller first step.
examples.whatToDo: Romain rewrites the coaching note around the action moment. He asks where the cue appeared, how hard the first move felt, and what size would fit.
examples.whyItMatters: A coach can be warm and still aim at the wrong part. The Stanford University Behavior Design frame keeps care tied to a concrete repair.

examples.title: The Learner Moves the Cue
examples.scenario: Cedric drags the practice card under Prompt while the rest of the onboarding class is still naming Motivation. He has been trying to start a water habit after lunch, yet the bottle stays in his bag. B=MAP is on the board with Motivation, Ability, Prompt, but the confusion is useful: the Stanford Behavior Design Lab model only helps when Cedric places the cue where lunch actually ends.
examples.whatToDo: Cedric moves the bottle beside the lunch tray and keeps the action to one sip. The teacher lets the class see how the formula changes a real cue.
examples.whyItMatters: Learning the words is not the same as using the model. The Fogg Behavior Model works when the learner changes one element in the moment.

examples.title: The Stuck Closet Reset
examples.scenario: The closet door sticks halfway, and Gwen has to tug the shoes free before the morning walk can even begin. Earlier, her Stanford University Behavior Design plan asked for a full workout, and the stuck door was enough friction to end it. Later, with the same hallway and the same shoes, she chooses one stretch by the closet. The coaching base behind the method spans over 60,000 people and 20 years of research.
examples.whatToDo: Gwen changes only Ability. She keeps the cue by the closet but shrinks the move until the sticky door no longer decides the morning.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-later view makes the repair visible. Behavior Design does not ask for a new personality when a smaller action will fit.

examples.title: The Buzz at the Table
examples.scenario: The phone buzzes at the pass against the restaurant's warm metal after closing service, and Aspen flinches before the health reminder opens. "So the prompt exists," Bonnie says. "Then why did I skip it?" Aspen asks. "B=MAP has 3 parts: Motivation, Ability, Prompt. Which one was weak?" The answer is not the cue. The Fogg Behavior Model, referenced by over 1,900 academic publications, sends them back to the action size.
examples.whatToDo: Aspen keeps the reminder but cuts the task to the first small move. Bonnie asks the MAP question again before either of them adds pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: The talk keeps the repair practical. A prompt can arrive and still fail when Motivation is low or Ability is too hard right then.

questions.prompt: A week after Pascal decides to take vitamins after breakfast, the bottle is still unopened beside the coffee tin. Which first read fits B=MAP?
choices: His decision is sincere, but breakfast may lack a prompt or easy first move.
His decision should work once he repeats it with more force each morning before breakfast.
His decision needs a longer goal statement so the habit feels serious enough at breakfast.
questions.explanation: B=MAP says a behavior needs Motivation, Ability, and Prompt in the same moment. A sincere decision can still fail when the cue or ease is absent.

questions.prompt: After a class demo, Madeline points to the whiteboard and says, "B=MAP is just a catchy motivation line." Which reply best corrects her reading?
choices: It gives Madeline a phrase to repeat when her class energy drops.
It helps Madeline compare which habit goal sounds most inspiring.
It gives Madeline three variables to inspect when a behavior fails.
questions.explanation: The model is diagnostic, not a slogan. The formula points Madeline toward Motivation, Ability, and Prompt rather than a pep line.

questions.prompt: During a coaching debrief, Bonnie calls the model a private coaching trick after hearing one success story. What evidence changes that claim?
choices: The model lets Bonnie make a private plan before telling anyone.
Over 1,900 academic publications are reported as referencing the model.
The model sounds simple enough for Bonnie to remember without notes.
questions.explanation: The publication count shows a broader academic footprint. A private plan or easy phrase would not answer Bonnie's claim about scope.

questions.prompt: Romain reads a training note and says the method sounds like a pile of personal anecdotes. Which source link most directly pushes back?
choices: The method is tied to Stanford behavior design work and the Behavior Design Lab.
The method gives Romain a gentler way to talk about his missed habit after practice.
The method works best when Romain keeps his example small and concrete.
questions.explanation: The Stanford and Behavior Design Lab link supports a research-and-training frame. The other choices may be useful, but they do not answer the anecdote claim.

questions.prompt: While Gwen plans a small evening habit, a coworker says the method must be a quick launch fad. Which answer uses the source best?
choices: Gwen can make the plan feel less like a fad by choosing a more impressive habit.
Gwen can wait until the plan is popular enough that the launch story matters less.
The method draws on 20 years of research, so the quick-launch story fails.
questions.explanation: The 20-year research period contradicts the quick-launch story. Bigger habits and popularity do not answer the source claim.

questions.prompt: Cedric is sorting a failed habit in a coaching worksheet and thinks the method was tested only through a few famous cases. Which reply fits the record?
choices: The method would look stronger if Cedric found one famous person who used it.
The source names over 60,000 coached people, not a handful of elites.
The method can still help Cedric if his own habit is ordinary and private.
questions.explanation: The source points to over 60,000 personally coached people. That directly answers Cedric's celebrity-case misread.

questions.prompt: Aspen wants to check in on a friend after dinner but keeps missing it. The note is buried in a chat app. Which MAP diagnosis should come first?
choices: The prompt is buried, even if Aspen cares and the check-in is easy.
The check-in needs a larger promise so Aspen treats the friendship as more serious.
The missed message means Aspen should wait for stronger concern before acting.
questions.explanation: B=MAP checks the action moment. Aspen may have Motivation and Ability, but a buried prompt can still block the check-in.

questions.prompt: Bonnie's team treats B=MAP as a motto on a poster beside the signup laptop. The signup still fails after the meeting. Which use fits the model?
choices: Repeat the motto before the next signup push so the team sounds aligned.
Choose the most inspiring habit goal and make the poster easier to see.
Use the formula to inspect Motivation, Ability, and Prompt.
questions.explanation: B=MAP is the model's diagnostic expression. A poster motto does not inspect the failed signup moment.

questions.prompt: Madeline sets a calendar reminder for a stretch, but the stretch still feels too hard after work. What should she inspect next?
choices: She should make the reminder louder so the calendar proves she meant it.
She should raise Ability by making the first move easier.
She should write a stronger reason so effort feels worthy after work.
questions.explanation: The prompt exists, so the next likely MAP repair is Ability. A louder cue or stronger reason misses the hard first move.

reviewCards.front: What three parts must meet for B=MAP to produce a behavior?
reviewCards.back: Motivation, Ability, and Prompt must arrive in the same moment. If one is missing or weak, a sincere decision may still fail to become action.

reviewCards.front: Why is B=MAP more than a motivational slogan?
reviewCards.back: It is a diagnostic formula. When a behavior fails, it sends you to inspect three variables instead of repeating a pep phrase.

reviewCards.front: What does the over-1,900 publication detail help establish?
reviewCards.back: It shows the Fogg Behavior Model has an academic footprint beyond one private coaching setting, so the model is not just a personal trick.

reviewCards.front: How does the Stanford Behavior Design link change the way you read failure?
reviewCards.back: It points you toward design variables rather than moral judgment. You ask what changed in Motivation, Ability, or Prompt.

reviewCards.front: Why does the over-60,000 coaching base matter for a tiny action?
reviewCards.back: It suggests the method was shaped through many ordinary behavior cases. The point is not celebrity proof, but repeated design practice.

reviewCards.front: What does 20 years of research add to the method's frame?
reviewCards.back: It makes the method read as tested design work rather than a quick launch fad. The repair still happens in one small action moment.

implementationPlan.title: Walk the MAP Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Walk the MAP Check when a behavior slips. Replay the exact moment and ask which part was weak: Motivation, Ability, or Prompt. Choose one repair small enough to try the next time the same cue appears.

ifThenPlans.context: If you feel the pull to skip a tiny action
ifThenPlans.plan: If you feel that pull, then Walk the MAP Check for a few steps and name the missing part before you change the habit.

ifThenPlans.context: If a reminder fires and you still avoid the behavior
ifThenPlans.plan: If the cue shows up but you stall, then Walk the MAP Check and shrink the action before adding another reminder.

ifThenPlans.context: If the action needs a large block of time
ifThenPlans.plan: If the time block feels too large, then Walk the MAP Check and cut the first move until it can fit a short opening.

ifThenPlans.context: If you start calling the miss a character flaw
ifThenPlans.plan: If the self-blame story starts, then Walk the MAP Check and write one design variable you can alter.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: The next time you feel the pull to skip a chosen behavior, put a 10-minute block on your calendar, walk, and pick one MAP repair to test within the day.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Practice the same behavior 3 times this week with widening gaps: today, two days later, and near week's end. After each attempt, Walk the MAP Check and make the next repair easier, clearer, or more specific: shrink the first move, move the cue closer, or name the weak MAP element.

memorableLines.text: A skipped habit is a design clue.
memorableLines.why: It turns failure into a concrete inspection instead of a self-attack.

memorableLines.text: The right diagnosis saves effort.
memorableLines.why: It makes the model feel useful, not merely neat.

memorableLines.text: Behavior Design asks you to stop using shame as proof that you care.
memorableLines.why: It names the emotional cost of applying the model.

chapters.title: Motivation-Focus on Matching
chapters.hook: What if the packed gym bag is not proof of grit, but a bridge to your weaker day?
chapters.counterintuition: A surge of drive feels like permission to go big. In fact, the best use of that surge is often to make the later action small.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next task handoff, rename one note or tab: "Teach one person: match the action to today's drive." Use your real next habit.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use high motivation to set up easy behavior, then shrink the habit until it still works when your drive has dropped. That is motivation matching at street level.

breakdown.fastRead:
A packed gym bag by the door feels like a promise. You picture a full workout, a clean meal, a better week. Then the wave drops, and the bag becomes clutter.

High drive is borrowed weather. Use it to make tomorrow's action smaller, not to make a bigger vow. If you feel hope, prep the easy path: fill the bottle, set shoes where your foot lands, pick one stretch. If drive is low, choose the action that can cross the line now.

Match the action to the day. Motivation matching means sizing the behavior to the drive you actually have. Tiny survives when giant quits.
breakdown.deepRead:
A statue can pull you before you know why. In Oslo's Vigeland Sculpture Park, the motivation photos make the point plain: drive is not one lump of willpower. It comes from Sensation, Anticipation, and Belonging.

Sensation is body-level pull: pleasure/pain. A sore back can make stretching feel urgent. A warm shower can make the same stretch easy to skip. Anticipation is future pull: hope/fear. You act because you see a better result coming, or because you want to dodge a bad one. Belonging is social pull: acceptance/rejection. You may show up because the group matters to you, or because being left out stings.

Those pulls rise and fall. Brielle can want a long run when hope is high after a race video. By dinner, the same run can feel absurd. Nothing about her character changed. The available motivation changed.

That is why matching beats pumping yourself up. When drive is high, do a harder setup action. Put the shoes by the door. Buy the floss. Move the app to the first screen. When drive is low, ask for the tiny version you can still do. One stretch. One tooth. One line.

The wave gives the timing. The crest can lift the heavy setup for a short while. The low part leaves easy things. Your job is not to freeze the crest. Your job is to use it before it fades.
breakdown.fullRead:
Wade has seen the Sunday version of himself make bold plans. That version buys vegetables, lines up workout clothes, and writes a budget note with neat boxes. By Wednesday night, after the commute and the late message, the same plan feels like it came from a stranger.

The 2012 health conference framing of the Motivation Wave gives that stranger problem a name. High motivation can carry hard things. Low motivation leaves easy things. You have felt both. You have signed up for a course while excited, then stared at the first long lesson after a hard day. You have promised a full cleanup, then moved one sock and quit.

Respect for the low day is the start. It does not sneer at the high day. The high day is useful. Use it to lower friction. If you feel a rush to get healthy, do not spend it only on a heroic promise. Spend some of it on setup: put the medicine where you will see it, wash the water bottle, choose the smallest starter action.

Then write the action for the low day. Not the action you wish you would do. The action you can do when you are tired, annoyed, late, or bored. This is where many plans leak money and time. You buy the annual app while the wave is high, but the daily lesson stays too large. A month later, the renewal charge lands, and the habit is still mostly a wish.

The three Core Motivators help you tell what kind of wave you are riding. If the pull is Sensation, check the body: pleasure, pain, ease, discomfort. If the pull is Anticipation, check the picture in your head: hope or fear. If the pull is Belonging, check the social edge: acceptance or rejection. The label does not solve the habit. It tells you what fuel is present, so you do not pretend it will last all week.

Russell's best plan for a low-drive night is not Russell's best plan for a fresh morning. On the fresh morning, he can do the harder setup. He can pack the food, clear the floor, or ask a friend to walk. On the low-drive night, he needs the smaller action. Open the container. Put on the shoes. Walk to the hallway and back.

There is a time to do the opposite. If the action is urgent and cannot be made tiny without dodging the real need, do not hide inside a token step. If a bill is due today, writing the envelope title is not enough. If someone needs a ride now, opening the map is not the whole job. Ask for help, cancel something, or do the hard action.

This sizing move is for building habits, not for excusing avoidable neglect. Use it when repetition matters and the behavior can be sized. Use the wave to make the next repeat easy. Then let the tiny action do what the huge promise could not.

examples.title: Program On The Table
examples.scenario: Oliver folds the 2012 health conference program beside two empty coffee cups while Maxime offers a hard-things workout plan after the Motivation Wave keynote. Oliver says no before anything starts. The hour could go to choosing a gym, buying gear, or setting one easy thing for tomorrow. They keep the plan on the table and talk only about what the low part of the wave will still allow.
examples.whatToDo: Oliver asks Maxime to turn the offer into setup, not pressure. They name one easy thing that can repeat after the keynote feeling fades.
examples.whyItMatters: High motivation can pay for hard things, but the repeat has to survive ordinary drive. The help works only after it is resized.

examples.title: Reply All Pledge
examples.scenario: Maxime is three words into a reply-all pledge in the email when another note asks every 2012 health conference attendee to join a month of hard things. He weighs two bad options: saying yes protects his public face, while saying no wastes the Motivation Wave in front of peers. Brielle offers a tracking sheet. Maxime refuses because the sheet makes the hard thing louder, then asks her to rewrite the pledge around one easy thing.
examples.whatToDo: Maxime answers with the smaller pledge and asks Brielle to cut the sheet down to one daily mark. He keeps the public promise tied to a low-drive action.
examples.whyItMatters: A public wave can push you into a plan built for applause. Reshaping the help keeps belonging from becoming an oversized habit.

examples.title: Bus Leaves Soon
examples.scenario: There is no time to tour every statue before the bus leaves Oslo's Vigeland Sculpture Park. Teacher Brielle points to three photos. "They all look like motivation." Guide Russell says, "Sort the pull first: Sensation, Anticipation, Belonging." Brielle taps the pleasure/pain photo, then the hope/fear photo. "So the same habit may need a different size depending on which pull is live."
examples.whatToDo: Brielle names the pull before choosing the action size. She stops treating every urge as one willpower meter.
examples.whyItMatters: Sensation, Anticipation, and Belonging turn vague drive into something you can read. Once you know the pull, you can size the habit.

examples.title: Wrong Photo Wins
examples.scenario: Every photo from Oslo's Vigeland Sculpture Park seemed strong enough to sell a bigger walking plan. Guide Russell expected the pleasure/pain image to win when teacher Brielle asked visitors to choose at the park gate. The reveal surprised him: the Sensation, Anticipation, Belonging set pulled different answers, and the acceptance/rejection photo led people toward one shared lap instead of the grand solo route.
examples.whatToDo: Russell changes the prompt from "Which image is strongest?" to "Which pull will still support the smallest next walk?"
examples.whyItMatters: The biggest feeling is not always the best habit size. Belonging may call for a tiny shared action rather than a dramatic solo plan.

examples.title: One Glass Thread
examples.scenario: "They'll quit when the conference feeling fades," someone says behind Wade, and he stops typing the wellness form due tonight. Wade texts Florent: "Want the full hard-things plan from the 2012 health conference?" Florent: "No. I am cooked." Wade: "Motivation Wave version: one easy thing after the drop?" Florent: "One glass of water before coffee."
examples.whatToDo: Wade replaces the full plan with one text line Florent can say yes to. The help lands because it asks for an easy thing.
examples.whyItMatters: A compressed thread can expose the mismatch fast. The right help does not add energy; it fits the energy that is there.

examples.title: Boots Off Reset
examples.scenario: "Start over," Hadley says, and Florent closes the budget app in the hallway between bedrooms. The 2012 health conference clip has just shown the Motivation Wave, with hard things riding high and easy things surviving low. Florent's old routine begins with a long review after work. He refuses Hadley's color-coded sheet. Then he restarts with one easy thing: write the balance before his boots come off.
examples.whatToDo: Florent stops the old review, writes one balance line, and leaves the larger budget work for a higher-drive window.
examples.whyItMatters: A reset is not a speech. It is the moment you stop a mismatched routine and restart at the size your drive can carry.

questions.prompt: "Motivation is just wanting it badly enough," a coworker says while picking a new habit. Which reply best matches the model?
choices: Name the pull first: Sensation, Anticipation, or Belonging may be doing the work.
Raise desire first, since motivation is one drive that needs stronger reasons and a louder goal.
Skip the motive first, since action size and prompts are the only parts worth checking.
questions.explanation: The model separates motivation into three Core Motivators. Treating it as one drive pushes the coworker toward force instead of diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Your running plan depends on the rush you feel after buying new shoes. The first sore week arrives. Which motive did the plan fail to size for?
choices: The plan treated a future runner identity as the only force worth tracking.
The plan treated social approval from other runners as the force worth tracking.
The plan ignored pleasure and pain as a near-term force worth tracking.
questions.explanation: Sensation includes pleasure/pain. A plan that ignores sore feet may look strong on goal day and fail when the body starts voting.

questions.prompt: A coach tells a nervous beginner, "Hope and fear are too messy for habit design." Which correction fits the model?
choices: Hope and fear belong under Anticipation, so future expectation can pull action.
Hope and fear sit outside the model, so the coach should size only effort and time.
Hope and fear count only after the beginner repeats the habit for several weeks.
questions.explanation: Anticipation names hope/fear as part of motivation. The coach is wrong to treat future expectation as outside habit design.

questions.prompt: A student flosses only before dental visits because roommates tease dirty teeth. What is easy to miss in that pattern?
choices: Pleasure and pain are the whole motive, so the roommates are background noise.
Acceptance and rejection can drive the behavior through Belonging.
Hope and fear explain the entire pattern once the visit is scheduled.
questions.explanation: Belonging includes acceptance/rejection. The social edge may be the live motive, not just a side detail around the dental visit.

questions.prompt: A trainer says, "I invented the Motivation Wave for my Tuesday class." What should you correct without overstating it?
choices: The phrase should be read as a private class label with no dated setting behind it.
The concept has a 2012 health conference anchor, so it is not just her label.
The phrase should be limited to medical behavior and kept away from daily habits.
questions.explanation: The source gives the Motivation Wave a 2012 health conference setting. That corrects the origin claim without adding claims the source does not make.

questions.prompt: After a fund-raiser, a volunteer feels a surge and wants to change everything. Which setup best uses the high part of the Motivation Wave?
choices: Save the harder setup action for a tired day so it proves commitment under pressure.
Use the surge to handle a harder setup action that makes later steps easier.
Skip setup and pick the daily action only after the surge is gone.
questions.explanation: High motivation can support hard behavior for a short window. Saving hard setup for a low-energy day reverses the wave's lesson.

questions.prompt: "Once I choose the goal, the drive will stay," a friend says. What should you expect when ordinary days return?
choices: Drive will stay high if the goal was chosen in public and praised by friends.
Drive will rise each day once the first plan is written.
Drive will drop, so only an easy version is likely to last.
questions.explanation: The wave metaphor says motivation subsides. A lasting design needs an easy version for the low part, not faith that drive will remain high.

questions.prompt: In a habit group chat, one person wants comfort, one fears missing a deadline, and one wants to feel included. Which sorting helps first?
choices: Sort the pulls as Sensation, Anticipation, and Belonging before choosing behavior size.
Merge the pulls into willpower and ask everyone to try with equal force before changing the plan.
Ignore the pulls and choose one habit size for the whole group to keep the chat simple.
questions.explanation: The three named motivators let the group diagnose different pulls. A single willpower label hides useful differences.

questions.prompt: A team launches a wellness pledge during a high-energy kickoff and keeps the daily task hard. Which later result should not surprise them?
choices: The pledge improves because hard actions train motivation to stay high after the kickoff.
The pledge holds because kickoff energy usually becomes the new baseline for the team.
The pledge fades when the wave drops because hard daily actions no longer fit.
questions.explanation: After motivation drops, only easy things remain realistic. The pledge was designed for the kickoff, not for the lower-drive days after it.

reviewCards.front: What are the three Core Motivators, and why name them before sizing a habit?
reviewCards.back: They are Sensation, Anticipation, and Belonging. Naming the pull tells you what kind of motivation is present before you choose how small the action should be.

reviewCards.front: What does the high part of the Motivation Wave let you do?
reviewCards.back: It can carry harder setup actions for a short time. Use that window to make the next repeat easier, such as placing the tool or cutting the first step down.

reviewCards.front: Why should a habit shrink after the Motivation Wave drops?
reviewCards.back: Motivation does not stay at the crest. When it falls, only easy actions remain realistic, so the repeat needs a tiny version built for ordinary drive.

reviewCards.front: Where does B=MAP behavior diagnosis (Ch 1) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: It helps you check the action moment: motivation, ability, and prompt still need to meet. It misleads if you use the formula to chase more motivation instead of shrinking the behavior for a low-drive day.

reviewCards.front: How do Sensation, Anticipation, and Belonging differ in plain words?
reviewCards.back: Sensation is pleasure or pain now. Anticipation is hope or fear about what may happen. Belonging is the pull of acceptance or the sting of rejection.

reviewCards.front: What common mistake does motivation matching prevent?
reviewCards.back: It stops you from using a high-drive moment to choose an oversized habit. Use the wave for setup, then pick a repeat you can still do when energy is ordinary.

implementationPlan.title: Write the Match Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice writing one line before you pick the size of a habit. The line names the moment, the current drive, and the smallest useful action. This is not a pep talk. It is a sizing move.

ifThenPlans.context: Your first plan sounds like a full workout, full lesson, or full cleanup.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first plan sounds full-size, then Write the Match Line: "For this moment, the tiny version is ____."

ifThenPlans.context: A surge of hope arrives after a class, video, talk, or clean bill of health.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the surge is high, then Write the Match Line for setup: "I will make tomorrow easier by ____."

ifThenPlans.context: You feel flat at a transition between tasks.
ifThenPlans.plan: If your drive is low at a handoff, then Write the Match Line with one action you can finish before you leave the spot.

ifThenPlans.context: Someone offers you a chart, app, or routine that feels too big.
ifThenPlans.plan: If help lands too heavy, then Write the Match Line and ask them to reshape the help around that smaller action.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, at one handoff between tasks, write one Match Line for a real habit: "When my drive is ____, the tiny action is ____."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For a week, keep a three-column daily log: Moment, drive level, matched tiny action. Circle the action you still did on your lowest-drive day.

memorableLines.text: High drive is borrowed weather.
memorableLines.why: It gives motivation a simple shape without shaming the reader.

memorableLines.text: Match the action to the day.
memorableLines.why: It turns the idea into a line the reader can use at a real moment.

memorableLines.text: Tiny survives when giant quits.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the low-motivation lesson into one portable contrast.

chapters.title: Ability-Easy Does It
chapters.hook: How can the cookbook sit open on the counter while takeout wins again?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does shrinking a habit work when trying harder feels braver? Ability rises when the tightest resource gets lighter.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next habit attempt, say aloud, "The tight spot is ___." Then jot the resource you lacked.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit feels hard, do not scold yourself; rank the scarce resources, find the weakest link, and make that part easier before asking for more discipline.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why does Willow's cookbook sit open while cooking at home still feels out of reach? The recipe is clear, but dinner is still hard. The weak link may be time, clean pans, grocery money, tired feet, or a routine with no slot.

Ability means you can do the behavior here and now. If the action asks for the one thing you do not have, the action is not simple yet. Ease beats grit when grit is the wrong tool.

Start smaller at the tight spot. Chop one carrot. Open one recipe. Put one pan on the stove. A tiny habit is a design choice. You are not shrinking the goal because you are weak. You are shrinking the action until it can happen.
breakdown.deepRead:
Zachary's gym sign-up sheet says, "Train harder," and that sounds useful until the first new member goes blank. More skill can help, but it is the slow path when the behavior has not started.

There are three Ability Paths: Train, Tool or resource, and Scale back. Train means you teach the person a skill. Tool or resource means the world helps them do it. Scale back means the target behavior gets smaller. The three paths are not equal in daily life. Training often asks for more work before the first win.

That is why a cookbook matters. It is a tool or resource for cooking at home. It does not make Willow a better person. It cuts one hard part: deciding what to cook and how to do the next step. If the cookbook sits under a pile, it is not a tool yet. If it opens to one easy recipe before she shops, it raises ability.

Scale back is the Tiny Habits move. Instead of "work out," do two wall pushups. Instead of "clean the kitchen," wipe one counter. The smaller move needs less time, less physical effort, and fewer brain cycles. The behavior can cross the line from good idea to done action.

The weakest link gets the first redesign. If time is tight, shrink the minutes. If money is tight, use what is already in the room. If brain cycles are gone, make the next step visible. You are not proving devotion. You are making the behavior easy enough to begin.
breakdown.fullRead:
Douglas writes the memo after the video-call waiting room freezes for the third time. The team wants a new habit: send a quick check-in after each client call. The first draft says, "Everyone should remember." That line fails before anyone tries it.

The Ability Chain gives Douglas a better question: which link is tight right now? The image uses five factors, and its point is not a bigger checklist. A chain breaks at the weakest link, not at the link with the best slogan. Time can be the block. Money can be the block. Physical effort can be the block. Brain cycles can be the block. The useful move is to find the tight link instead of polishing every link.

A behavior can be simple in one place and hard in another. Two wall pushups after a bathroom trip may feel easy at home. The same two pushups in a busy office hall may feel strange. The action is short, but the moment does not fit. Short is not the same as easy.

This is where random shrinking goes wrong. If Nova cannot cook because groceries cost too much this week, "cook one smaller dinner" may still miss the block. The money link is tight. A pantry meal, a shared ingredient, or a cheaper recipe helps more than a tiny version of an expensive plan.

The same thing happens with brain cycles. Madelyn can know the habit and still miss it when her phone is at 1% before a drive, her charger is gone, and the address is in a message she meant to answer. The hard part is not desire. It is the next step vanishing when attention is already spent.

Rank the links before you fix the habit. Ask which resource is scarcest in the exact moment: time, money, physical effort, or brain cycles. If the action is brief and still slips, ask whether it has a real place in the day. Then make only that part easier first. Put the floss beside the sink. Choose the cheaper meal. Say the sentence before the call. Move the habit after something that already happens.

This protects you from two bad stories. One says you need more discipline. The other says every habit should be tiny forever. Neither is careful enough. Sometimes you need a tool. Sometimes you need a smaller action. Sometimes you need a better place in the routine.

Good support names the missing support before it shrinks anything. The idea misleads the coach who uses tiny as an excuse to under-support people. If a learner needs a real tool, money, safety, or training, shrinking alone can sound kind while leaving the real block in place.

examples.title: Front Desk Paths
examples.scenario: The trainer with the sign-up tablet gets called to the pool, and Zachary is left at the gym front desk with Marshall beside the towel bin. "So I tell them to train people?" Zachary asks. Marshall taps the form. "One of the 3 paths. You can train people, give a tool or resource, or scale back the target behavior." A new member waits with a blank waiver and wet shoes.
examples.whatToDo: Zachary changes the sign-up script. He asks which of the 3 paths fits first, then offers a tool or resource or a scaled-back target before he suggests training.
examples.whyItMatters: Training can help, but it is often the hard path. A coach who sees all 3 paths can raise ability before the new member feels behind.

examples.title: Cookbook Turnaround
examples.scenario: Willow is sliding the heavy pot back into the cabinet while the cookbook stays open to a long recipe for cooking at home. Her thumb hovers over another takeout order. Then she catches the error: she used the cookbook as pressure to cook well, not as a tool or resource that makes behavior easier. The recipe did not fail her. The next step was too large.
examples.whatToDo: Willow turns to a one-pan page and writes the first move on a scrap: rinse the rice. The cookbook becomes a tool or resource for one easier action.
examples.whyItMatters: A tool only raises ability when it lowers the next bit of effort. If the cookbook adds pressure, it has stopped making behavior easier.

examples.title: Waiting Room Memo
examples.scenario: The laptop hinge sticks halfway, and Douglas types the memo with the camera still off: "Client check-in habit. Our Ability Chain is not failing from desire. Weakest link: brain cycles after hard calls. Time and money are fine. Decision: stop asking people to remember. Add a two-word draft in the call notes before the next window opens."
examples.whatToDo: Douglas sends the memo as a work log. He names brain cycles as the weakest link and changes the habit so the first words are already in the notes.
examples.whyItMatters: The Ability Chain keeps the fix aimed. If the weak link is brain cycles, adding time or money will not make the follow-up easier.

examples.title: Garden Link Split
examples.scenario: The tomato starts were limp this evening before the watering list reached the community garden shed. Volunteer Carmen brought a new hose and solved physical effort; the walk was shorter, the spray lighter. Volunteer Nova used the Ability Chain differently. She wrote, "Weakest link: not time and money." Watering had no steady place in the day, so she tied it to locking the gate. One bed got water. One got a better tool nobody remembered to use.
examples.whatToDo: Carmen improves the tool. Nova names the weakest link and changes where the act fits in the day.
examples.whyItMatters: Opposite fixes can both look sensible. The habit follows the tight spot, so a better tool loses when the routine still has no place.

examples.title: Recipe Reframe
examples.scenario: Parent Madelyn sets the grocery bag on the passenger seat instead of carrying it inside after school pickup. Her late reply to Carmen is still unsent in the parked car, and the cookbook feels like proof she is bad at cooking at home. Marshall hears that over the car speaker and says, "A tool only helps when it makes the next move lighter." Madelyn opens to a soup page with one pot and one first chop.
examples.whatToDo: Madelyn stops treating the cookbook as a verdict. She uses it as a tool or resource and picks the recipe that makes behavior easier right now.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe removes shame from the tool. A cookbook is useful when it lowers effort, not when it proves cooking at home should be easy already.

examples.title: Three Path Lesson
examples.scenario: Teacher Marshall erases the full workout plan on the board in the community college classroom while Zachary is still copying it. "Did you just make the goal smaller?" Zachary asks. Marshall writes 3 paths: train people, tool or resource, scale back the target behavior. The room stops treating Tiny Habits as a weak promise and starts sorting which path fits the stuck behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Marshall gives each learner a stuck behavior and asks for the first easier version. The class must name the path before changing the assignment.
examples.whyItMatters: Confusion is the material. Once learners see all 3 paths, scale back becomes a design move inside Tiny Habits, not a fake win.

questions.prompt: Zachary says, "Ability means we train people harder first," while Marshall points to a stalled habit plan. Which answer fits the ability page?
choices: The plan should begin with training because skill is the only dependable way to raise ability.
The plan should avoid tools until people show enough commitment to practice the behavior.
The plan can use training, a tool or resource, or a scaled-back behavior to raise ability.
questions.explanation: The source names 3 paths, not one. Training is one path, but tools and scaling back are also official ways to make action easier.

questions.prompt: Marshall schedules a long skill class before anyone tries the two-pushup habit. Which result should he expect if training comes first?
choices: The habit may gain friction because training asks for skill work before the behavior can start.
The habit may become simple because training is the easiest path on the ability page.
The habit may stop needing a prompt because trained people remember more reliably.
questions.explanation: Training can work, but the source calls it the hard path. It can add work before the first small action happens.

questions.prompt: During the garden reset, Nova sees Carmen buy a lighter hose and says, "Tools distract people from real habit change." What does that line miss before they choose the watering habit?
choices: A tool matters only after the person has enough motivation to finish the full behavior.
A tool can raise ability by lowering effort before motivation or new skill changes.
A tool works best when it makes the habit feel more serious to the group.
questions.explanation: The ability page includes tools and resources. A tool is not a side issue when it makes the behavior easier to do.

questions.prompt: Willow is standing by the apartment stove with the cookbook open, and she shrinks "cook dinner" to "rinse the rice." Which reading matches Tiny Habits?
choices: The smaller action counts because scaling back is the Tiny Habits path for making behavior easier.
The smaller action counts only after Willow proves she can cook the whole recipe later.
The smaller action counts when it feels harder than the behavior she first avoided.
questions.explanation: The source links scale-back to Tiny Habits. A smaller target can cross the action line because it uses less scarce resource.

questions.prompt: "The cookbook only makes me want to cook," Madelyn says from the driveway. What should she change in that reading?
choices: She should see the cookbook as a reward after cooking at home has already become steady.
She should see the cookbook as a resource that lowers decision and knowledge friction.
She should see the cookbook as a training plan that replaces the need to scale back.
questions.explanation: The cookbook example is about ability, not motivation. It helps by making cooking at home easier to choose and start.

questions.prompt: Carmen can water the garden easily after work, but the same task feels hard on a rushed morning. Which account explains the shift?
choices: The behavior has one true difficulty, so one of Carmen's reports is probably inaccurate.
The behavior changes only when Carmen's motivation rises or falls between those moments.
The behavior can be simple or hard depending on which resource is scarce right then.
questions.explanation: Simplicity depends on the scarcest resource at the moment. The same act can feel easy in one setting and hard in another.

questions.prompt: "I know how to do it, so ability is not the issue," Douglas says after skipping a paid class errand. Which reply fits the model?
choices: Ability is settled once Douglas has the physical skill, even when the errand costs money.
Ability is mostly about confidence, so Douglas should practice the errand in his head.
Ability can still be blocked when time or money is the scarce resource.
questions.explanation: The source names time and money as ability resources. Knowing how to act does not remove a concrete cost or schedule block.

questions.prompt: Nova reads the Ability Chain and wants every factor perfected before the first try. Which next move uses the chain well?
choices: She should find the weakest link and ease that factor before fixing the rest.
She should improve every link equally so no factor can be blamed later.
She should ignore the chain until the habit has failed several times.
questions.explanation: Use the chain to find the weakest link. The useful fix targets the limiting factor instead of asking every factor to be perfect.

questions.prompt: A habit takes only a few seconds, but Madelyn keeps missing it when her day is crowded and the cue is new. What does that show?
choices: Short actions usually prove the person has enough ability and should work on motivation.
Short actions can still be hard when brain cycles or non-routine block the moment.
Short actions mainly fail when they cost money or require too much physical effort.
questions.explanation: Brain cycles and non-routine are ability constraints. A behavior can be brief and still too hard when the next step is not obvious.

reviewCards.front: A habit is stalled. How do the three Ability Paths help you pick a first fix?
reviewCards.back: They keep training from becoming the only answer. Train when skill is tight, give a tool or resource when support is missing, or scale back when the target is too big.

reviewCards.front: How does the Ability Chain tell you where to start?
reviewCards.back: Use it to compare the links in the moment. Do not fix every factor at once; find the link that is tight now and make that part easier first.

reviewCards.front: Why is a cookbook an ability tool, not a motivation tool?
reviewCards.back: A cookbook can lower decision and knowledge friction for cooking at home. It helps when it makes the next step easier, not when it merely inspires.

reviewCards.front: Why does scaling back fit Tiny Habits?
reviewCards.back: Scaling back lowers the resource needed for the target behavior. The tiny version can start now, which is why it belongs inside Tiny Habits.

reviewCards.front: Why can the same behavior be easy one day and hard the next?
reviewCards.back: Simplicity depends on the scarcest resource in the moment. Time, money, body effort, brain cycles, or routine fit can change from one context to another.

reviewCards.front: How would you connect B=MAP (Ch 1) to Rank the Weakest Link in one sentence?
reviewCards.back: B=MAP says behavior needs ability, and this move raises ability by finding the scarcest resource and making that link easier before the prompt arrives.

implementationPlan.title: Rank the Weakest Link
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice spotting which resource is tight before you change the habit. Rank the Weakest Link by checking time, money, physical effort, and brain cycles first. If the action is short but still slips, check whether it lacks a steady place in your routine. Then make that one link easier first.

ifThenPlans.context: If your first fix is a class, tutorial, or long skill plan.
ifThenPlans.plan: If training is your first fix, then pause and run Rank the Weakest Link. Use training only when skill is truly the tight link.

ifThenPlans.context: If a tool you bought is making you feel more behind.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the tool adds pressure, then name the next action it should make easier. Keep it only if it lowers that step.

ifThenPlans.context: If a habit worked yesterday but feels heavy today.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same behavior feels harder, then check which resource changed. Shrink the strain where the current day is tight.

ifThenPlans.context: If the behavior is short but still slips away.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the action is brief but missed, then check brain cycles and routine fit. Make the cue visible or move the act after something steady.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, before you start one habit you keep delaying, rank time, money, body effort, and brain cycles. Say, "The tightest link is ___." Record one easier version.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, stage one habit at its real cue. Run Rank the Weakest Link out loud, shrink only the tightest link, and try the tiny version once.

memorableLines.text: Ease beats grit when grit is the wrong tool.
memorableLines.why: It makes the anti-shame stance easy to repeat.

memorableLines.text: A tiny habit is a design choice.
memorableLines.why: It turns scaling back from surrender into design.

memorableLines.text: The weakest link gets the first redesign.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the Ability Chain into one usable sentence.

chapters.title: Prompts-The Power of After
chapters.hook: Your reminder buzzed, and you still skipped it. What if the buzz was the wrong helper?
chapters.counterintuition: A prompt is not a nag, but the moment a behavior can start. Put it after a real routine, and memory loses the job.
chapters.tryThisNow: For 10 minutes during your next conversation about a missed habit, move one object into view, name the missed prompt, and choose the next after-moment.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A good prompt does less than remind you: it lands after something real, asks for the first tiny action, and fits your motivation and ability right then.

breakdown.fastRead:
Your rent transfer was simple. You meant to do it after payday, then a work chat, a grocery run, and a tired ride home filled the space. No prompt told the behavior to start now, so the money sat while the due date passed. Memory is a weak prompt.

A prompt is the cue that says now: an email, a request, a button, or the routine you already do. The strongest after-moment is plain. After I set the mug down, I will take the pill. After I open the laptop, I will write one line. The prompt does not carry the whole habit. It opens the first step.
breakdown.deepRead:
You need the cue at the same instant motivation, ability, and context can carry a tiny act. If it asks too much, the cue becomes noise.

Lorraine sees this in the BJ-Demo Facebook email. The account has been quiet, and her draft first asks the inactive user to get involved again. Lorraine is the expert on the screen, yet she hits her own limit. She can write an email prompt, but she cannot make involvement happen from one email. She can prompt sign into Facebook, then make that first step easy with a green sign-in button.

Olivia's worksheet gives the prompt types names. A Facilitator helps when motivation is present but ability needs help. A Signal simply says now when the person is ready. A Spark adds motivation when desire is low. One reminder cannot serve all three jobs.

Facebook respects the order. Log in comes before Find people you know on Facebook. Friends respond before the inactive user gets more involved. Ask for the first door, not the whole house. In your habits, that may mean one sip after the kettle clicks, not drink more water today. You are not weak for forgetting. The prompt was vague.
breakdown.fullRead:
The green button can fool you. It looks like a small design choice, almost too obvious to teach anything. Yet in the BJ-Demo email prompt, the button changes the ask. It does not say, become a daily user again. It says, sign into Facebook now, and makes that first move easy to see.

At home, use the same test. If your plan says read more, the prompt is still foggy. If it says after I put my keys in the bowl, I will read one paragraph, the cue has a place to land. Your hand touches the keys. The open page is there. The behavior is small enough to begin before your mood votes on it.

A prompt should match the person it meets. When the person wants to act but the step feels clumsy, build a Facilitator. Put the floss where the toothbrush already lives. When readiness is already there and only the start line is missing, use a Signal. The kettle clicks; you write the first sentence. When the person does not yet care enough, a Spark has to add a reason. A plain beep will not do that work.

Facebook's reinvolvement chain starts modestly for a reason. The 4-step behavior chain is not one giant shove. Log in, then find more friends, then friends respond, then more involvement can follow. If the first email tried to make Facebook a daily habit in one sentence, the prompt would be asking for the last step before the first one existed.

Your own after-moment needs the same humility. After lunch is not enough if lunch moves from the cafe to the car to your desk. After I close the lunch container is better because your hand has a real object. The prompt is not the hour. It is the thing you can notice without hunting for it.

Moving one object can make the cue visible. Put the pill bottle beside the toothbrush, or put the notebook on top of the laptop. The object is not a reward and not a moral test. It is a small sign that makes the after-moment visible before the day gets loud.

Wendy's appointment shows the cost when the prompt is missing. You meant to check on her. The day had enough care in it and enough love in it, but no now signal. By bedtime, the text is still unsent. The failure does not prove you care less. It proves memory was asked to do a job a prompt could have held.

The counter-case is concrete. If a medicine has to be taken inside a fixed window, do not depend only on after coffee if you sometimes skip coffee. Use the prompt form that fits the risk: an alarm, a request from another person, or a visible cue beside the dose. The lesson is not worship the routine. It is to make the start signal honest enough for the behavior.

examples.title: Draft Before Send
examples.scenario: The send window is closing, and product designer Lorraine is still in the draft for the BJ-Demo account. Her email prompt says, Come back and get involved, with a green sign-in button below it. The words snag. She notices her own error before the batch goes out: the prompt can ask someone to sign in, not become involved in one leap.
examples.whatToDo: Lorraine rewrites the email around the first action and leaves the green sign-in button as the easiest next move. She stops asking the prompt to carry the whole chain.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene keeps the prompt honest. If the ask is bigger than the next action, even a bright button becomes noise before the behavior starts.

examples.title: Type Chart Pause
examples.scenario: The prompt-type chart is tidy, but the reactivation email is not tidy at all. Olivia studies the 3 prompt types on the worksheet: Facilitator, Signal, Spark. Signal feels clean, she thinks, but the user may already know the service exists. Spark feels loud. The green sign-in button lowers effort, so her mind keeps circling back to Facilitator.
examples.whatToDo: Olivia names the job the prompt must do before she chooses the label. She treats Facilitator, Signal, and Spark as different fits, not as three words for reminder.
examples.whyItMatters: A prompt can fail while looking clear. The type matters because the same cue meets different mixes of motivation and ability.

examples.title: Calendar Invite Chain
examples.scenario: "It just needs to remind them," someone says behind Jude, and the shared calendar invite suddenly feels too short. He is planning the 4-step behavior chain: log in, Find people you know on Facebook, friends respond, then make Facebook a daily habit. The prompt has space for one clean ask. Before any email goes out, Jude gives the space to log in.
examples.whatToDo: Jude protects the first link. He plans the email prompt around log in and leaves friend-finding for the next screen, where the user can actually act on it.
examples.whyItMatters: Prompt space is scarce. When one cue tries to launch every later step, the first behavior has no clean doorway.

examples.title: Stronger Ask Doubt
examples.scenario: "Use the stronger ask," Raymond says on the BJ-Demo product review call, then hears how thin it sounds. One route asks the inactive user to find people before login; the other route asks only log in and risks seeming weak. He must pick before the email prompt is approved. Either way, he admits the prompt cannot make a daily habit by force.
examples.whatToDo: Raymond chooses the smaller ask and keeps the later social step out of the email. He lets the 4-step behavior chain start where the user can begin.
examples.whyItMatters: The expert move is the admission. A prompt that knows its own reach can start a chain; a prompt that pretends to finish it often blocks it.

examples.title: Three Type Exchange
examples.scenario: 3 prompt types. Evelyn writes the number on the whiteboard and stops. "Facilitator?" Wendy asks. "If the person wants to act but needs ease," Evelyn says. "Signal?" "If they are ready and need now." Wendy taps Spark. "When desire is low?" Evelyn nods. "Then the cue has to add a reason, not just wave."
examples.whatToDo: Evelyn makes Wendy test the user's state before picking the prompt type. The talk keeps Facilitator, Signal, and Spark tied to a real job.
examples.whyItMatters: A taxonomy helps only when it changes the design choice. The prompt should meet the user's missing piece, not the designer's favorite label.

examples.title: Reviewer Role Flip
examples.scenario: The usual email reviewer is out, so Phoebe gets the review screen in her inbox for the BJ-Demo account. She expects the lesson to be sharper copy. The reveal is quieter: the green sign-in button is doing real work. It turns the email prompt from a message into a visible way to sign in.
examples.whatToDo: Phoebe marks the button as part of the prompt, not decoration. She checks whether the first action is obvious enough to do without hunting.
examples.whyItMatters: The reader expects persuasion, but the prompt also changes ability. A cue can say now and make the now step easier.

questions.prompt: Your coworker points to a sore back and says, "I want to stretch daily, and I care a lot, so I will remember after work." What does this plan miss?
choices: The habit still needs a clear now signal before the stretch can start.
The stretch should stay larger so motivation has a reason to stay high.
The plan should wait until the person feels eager at the end of work.
questions.explanation: The model treats a prompt as required. Wanting the stretch does not supply the now signal, so the behavior can stay easy and desired yet still fail to start.

questions.prompt: While rebuilding a habit plan, Olivia deletes the mirror note and the after-coffee routine because only phone alerts seem official. What is she likely to lose?
choices: She loses useful prompts such as a routine, request, cue, or call to action.
She makes prompts stronger because phone alerts are the only real cue.
She avoids prompt clutter because daily routines are too vague to use.
questions.explanation: The source names many prompt forms, including routines and requests. Treating phones as the only prompt cuts away cues already built into the context.

questions.prompt: During a product review, someone says, "The prompt can be called a trigger because that is the current model term." Which correction fits the source?
choices: The older word still helps when a prompt is part of a product screen.
The current word matters only when prompts come from phone alerts.
The model now uses Prompt after the language changed in late 2017.
questions.explanation: The source distinguishes current language from older wording. Trigger is not the preferred current term after the late-2017 shift to Prompt.

questions.prompt: In a planning note, Raymond treats the BJ-Demo case as a calendar reminder someone set for themselves. Which detail breaks that reading?
choices: The BJ-Demo account had a weekly calendar alert after a quiet stretch.
The BJ-Demo account showed a saved reminder to sign in later.
Facebook sent the BJ-Demo account an email prompt after inactivity.
questions.explanation: A private reminder would come from the user's own calendar. Here Facebook sent an email prompt after the BJ-Demo account had gone unused.

questions.prompt: During the email review, someone says, "The message should ask the inactive user to become active again." What does that response overlook?
choices: It should start with finding friends because social action is the final goal.
It should ask for signing into Facebook because that is the first viable step.
It should ask for daily use because frequent return is the desired outcome.
questions.explanation: The prompt targets signing in, not full reinvolvement. Asking for the first viable step keeps the cue small enough to start the chain.

questions.prompt: On the review screen, Phoebe calls the green sign-in button decoration and focuses only on the email copy. Which reading is stronger?
choices: The button lowers effort, so the prompt also helps as a Facilitator.
The button adds motivation, so the prompt works mainly as a Spark.
The button marks timing, so the prompt is only a Signal.
questions.explanation: The green button makes the first action easier. That fits the Facilitator idea more than a mere Signal or a motivation-adding Spark.

questions.prompt: A team sends the same cue to one user who lacks ability, one who is ready, and one who lacks desire. What is most likely to go wrong?
choices: They can keep one reminder if the wording is short and clear.
They can favor Signal because it covers readiness and low ability.
They need to choose among Facilitator, Signal, and Spark by user state.
questions.explanation: The three prompt types exist because user states differ. One reminder can miss the user's real need: ease, timing, or motivation.

questions.prompt: The Facebook chain begins with login, then friend finding, friend response, and more involvement. What happens if the prompt skips login?
choices: The chain may still work if the later social ask feels more meaningful.
The chain loses its entry point because later steps depend on login first.
The chain should start with daily use because that is the desired state.
questions.explanation: The source maps the reinvolvement chain in steps. Later social actions depend on the first small behavior, so skipping login weakens the chain.

questions.prompt: Phoebe writes a prompt that asks a user to log in, find friends, invite people, and post an update. Which risk should she see first?
choices: The prompt may feel too small because it spends attention on login first.
The prompt may fail because a complicated ask adds friction at the cue.
The prompt may need more color because the ask lacks a visible button.
questions.explanation: The source warns against complicated asks at the prompt moment. A bigger request adds friction instead of helping the first behavior start.

reviewCards.front: Why can a wanted, easy behavior still disappear?
reviewCards.back: Because wanting and ease do not tell the behavior when to start. The missing piece is a prompt, the now signal that turns a possible action into the next action.

reviewCards.front: What are the three prompt types, and what does each one solve?
reviewCards.back: Facilitator helps ability, Signal marks the right moment, and Spark adds motivation. The type should match the user's state, not the designer's favorite cue.

reviewCards.front: Why is the green sign-in button more than decoration in the BJ-Demo Facebook email?
reviewCards.back: It lowers effort at the exact start point. The email prompt asks the BJ-Demo account to sign in, and the green sign-in button makes that first move easier.

reviewCards.front: How does the Facebook reinvolvement chain protect the first behavior?
reviewCards.back: It starts with login, then moves to finding friends, friends responding, and more involvement. The first prompt opens the chain instead of trying to finish it.

reviewCards.front: What does simplicity through the weakest link (Ch 3) get WRONG if you applied it naively to this case?
reviewCards.back: It may shrink the behavior but forget the now signal. In the Facebook case, signing in is small, yet it still needs an email prompt and a green sign-in button to start.

implementationPlan.title: Place the After Prompt
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice placing a tiny behavior after something that already happens. Use Place the After Prompt: name the routine, move one object to that spot, and ask for the first action only. If the prompt needs to help ease, timing, or desire, choose Facilitator, Signal, or Spark.

ifThenPlans.context: When you hear yourself say, I just need to remember
ifThenPlans.plan: If you hear that line, then Place the After Prompt by moving one visible object to the routine spot and naming the after-moment.

ifThenPlans.context: When your prompt asks for a whole outcome
ifThenPlans.plan: If the ask feels large, then Place the After Prompt around the first viable step and cut the later steps from the cue.

ifThenPlans.context: When the behavior depends on a message or request
ifThenPlans.plan: If another person is part of the start, then Place the After Prompt after the message you already send and ask for one clear reply.

ifThenPlans.context: When motivation is high but the action still feels clumsy
ifThenPlans.plan: If desire is present but ease is low, then Place the After Prompt as a Facilitator and move the needed object into the path.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, during one conversation about a habit you keep missing, move one small object toward the place the after-moment happens. Say, After I ___, I will ___.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person to flag the moment they hear you say, I need to remember, this week. Compare notes once and choose one after-prompt to place.

memorableLines.text: Memory is a weak prompt.
memorableLines.why: It makes the chapter's core warning short enough to recall before a habit slips.

memorableLines.text: Ask for the first door, not the whole house.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the Facebook chain lesson into an image you can use on any prompt.

memorableLines.text: A prompt should match the person it meets.
memorableLines.why: It gives the Facilitator, Signal, and Spark distinction a plain portable rule.

chapters.title: Emotions Create Habits
chapters.hook: 3 minutes a day, and the missed habit piece was the feeling after the tiny win.
chapters.counterintuition: You can do the tiny action and still miss the habit: the behavior happened, but the felt success did not.
chapters.tryThisNow: After your coffee, place one cue where your hand lands. Do the tiny step once and count the true win, not a cheer you have to fake.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A habit wires faster when success is felt right after the tiny action. Celebrate in a way that feels true, or shrink the action until the feeling can land.

breakdown.fastRead:
Nora flosses one tooth, drops the floss, and reaches for her phone. The tiny action happened. Nothing in her face changed. By lunch, the moment is gone, and the next repeat feels like one more task.

A habit needs a good feeling right after the behavior. Not a month later. Not after the whole goal. Right after. Feeling wires what repetition repeats.

That is why the Tiny Habits Recipe has three parts: Anchor, Behavior, Celebration. The win can be a smile, a quiet yes, or one calm breath. It must feel true. Celebration has to land.
breakdown.deepRead:
The small win has to arrive while the action is still warm. If Nora waits until Friday to praise a week of flossing, her body gets a receipt for Friday, not for the tooth she just cleaned.

John's public success report makes the rule small enough to use. He praises the Maui habit and says celebration is key. The lesson is not that the Maui habit has a lucky morning cue. The lesson is that the easy action and the good feeling are paired.

Deborah D names the gap from the other side. Other habit books had not tied habits with celebrations for her. That missing tie matters in the exact second after the behavior ends. If the moment passes without a felt win, the habit has less reason to call you back.

The public 5-Day guidance keeps the same order in miniature: focus on tiny and celebrate successes, big and small. Daily practice can take about 3 minutes Monday through Friday. Short practice keeps the win near the act, instead of burying it under a long course.

Shine is the felt lift after success. You can call it relief, pride, a grin, or a quiet yes. The name is less important than the timing. A tiny behavior followed by a true positive feeling becomes easier to repeat. A tiny behavior followed by nothing stays a chore.
breakdown.fullRead:
Caroline tries the rule too hard at first. She claps after every sip of water, then feels silly, then stops the habit and the celebration. The overcorrection is easy: if feeling good helps, more noise must help more.

Bradley tries a louder cheer at the bench and feels his face go hot. A fake victory teaches nothing. The feeling has to be real enough for you to believe it. A quiet breath can beat a loud cheer if the breath says, yes, I did the thing.

Nora's sink shows the exception that tests the rule. Celebrate after the tiny behavior, but do not force a celebration that rings false. If the win feels fake, shrink the behavior until success feels honest. One dish in the sink. One sentence in the draft. One stretch after the shoes come off.

Kathleen's renewal page shows the other risk. She can open the page today, but the saved money may not show up until later. If she waits to feel good until the charge disappears, the habit gets no help now. A small true win after opening the page gives the next action a reason to return.

Deborah D and another public success report point to the same pattern. Deborah connects celebrating a small win with looking forward to doing habits. The workout report pairs feeling Shine with not missing a day. The source does not ask you to earn a parade. It asks you to let the body feel a small yes while the behavior is still close.

Your tiny habit can need that feeling. People often try to run habits on duty alone, then wonder why the tiny act starts to feel like a bill. Emotion is not a bribe. It is the way the behavior becomes welcome.

Bradley's workshop bench adds the social part. He can say yes under his breath, but he freezes when Maurice is nearby. So the celebration may need to be private. A tiny nod, a thumb against a finger, or a silent word can do the job. The feeling counts even if nobody else sees it.

Alice's school form adds timing. If she finishes the form and celebrates later in the car, the feeling may attach to leaving school, not to finishing the form. Put the win as close as you can to the completed act. The habit recipe needs Anchor, Behavior, and Celebration in that order, not celebration floating around whenever the day calms down.

You are not taking on another demand. You are not required to feel thrilled about every tiny task. You are looking for one honest flicker of success. If the flicker is not there, the answer may be to make the action smaller or choose a celebration that fits your real mood.

When celebration becomes theater, stop performing and make the behavior smaller. The right celebration is not louder than the action. It is the first honest yes after it.

examples.title: Drawer Reset
examples.scenario: The bathroom drawer jams halfway as Nora reaches for the floss, and the old routine almost wins: yank, sigh, one tooth, move on. Alice says from the hall, "You did the tiny part. Where is the celebration?" Nora stops with the floss taut between two fingers. John's Maui habit report is on her mind: "Celebration is key." She closes the drawer, smiles for real, and starts the one-tooth habit again.
examples.whatToDo: Nora treats the pause as the practice. She restarts the tiny behavior, finishes one tooth, and lets a small true smile arrive before she leaves the sink.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset puts the good feeling beside the behavior. Without that felt success, the tiny action can become another task to survive.

examples.title: Warm Cup Win
examples.scenario: The paper cup warms Alice's palm while the parent-teacher conference line crawls past the table. Maurice says, "You finished the school form." Alice nods, but her face has already moved to the next errand. Deborah D. had said other habit books had not tied habits with celebrations. Alice lets the small win land before the next signature, a quiet "good" under her breath.
examples.whatToDo: Alice stays with the finished form for one breath. She does not add another task yet; she lets the completed tiny action feel complete.
examples.whyItMatters: The vignette shows the missing ingredient without drama. Celebration can be the small pause that lets success become something the reader wants again.

examples.title: Cap Before Click
examples.scenario: Workshop coach Bradley sets the marker cap on the workshop bench instead of snapping it shut during recipe practice. "John said the Maui habit worked because celebration is key," Maurice says. Bradley points at his habit recipe. "What if my cheer feels fake?" "Then it is not the celebration yet," Maurice says. "Find the smallest true feeling." Bradley writes "done" under the tiny behavior and lets the word warm before the cap clicks.
examples.whatToDo: Bradley keeps the rule but changes the size of the celebration. He stops pretending and waits for the smallest honest yes he can feel.
examples.whyItMatters: This is the rule meeting its exception. Celebration works as habit wiring only when the positive feeling actually reaches the person doing the act.

examples.title: Voicemail Catch
examples.scenario: Deleting the third voicemail after dinner, care-team volunteer Maurice gives himself a stiff thumbs-up and reaches for the next message. Kathleen hears the flat little clap through the speaker. "Did that feel good?" she asks. Maurice catches the error midstream. The Deborah D. success page said other books had not tied habits with celebrations or shown the move to celebrate a small win. He replays the tiny act and lets one honest breath count.
