examples.whatToDo: Maurice corrects the celebration, not the inbox. He lets the deleted message register as one completed tiny behavior before touching the next one.
examples.whyItMatters: Recovery begins at the noticing point. A performed celebration can look right and still fail to make the next repeat more inviting.

examples.title: Renewal Note
examples.scenario: Household budget lead Kathleen is three lines into the renewal-cancel note on the front stoop when the bank alert lands. Her memo reads: "Rule: celebrate right after the tiny action. Exception: not after the money is saved next month. John praised the Maui habit because celebration is key now. Decision: after I open the account page, I mark one real win before I keep searching." A margin reply lands: "Good. Make the feeling immediate."
examples.whatToDo: Kathleen writes the decision where she will see it again. She celebrates opening the account page, so the next search step is not waiting on a later result.
examples.whyItMatters: Money stakes can pull attention toward the outcome. The memo keeps the habit wired to the repeatable action that happens today.

examples.title: Two Market Bags
examples.scenario: The receipt curls out of the card reader at the farmers market stall while Joel folds his bag shut. "I'll celebrate after a week of lunches," he says, and the greens soften by Tuesday. At the next stall, Caroline buys one bunch, whispers "nice" before she leaves, and says Deborah D.'s success page was right: habits with celebrations need the move to celebrate a small win. The same errand gives Joel a future test and Caroline a feeling to repeat.
examples.whatToDo: Joel waits for the full streak. Caroline lets the first small win count before she leaves the stall. The split shows which feeling is available now.
examples.whyItMatters: Delayed pride can starve the next repeat. A small true celebration makes tomorrow's action more attractive before a full streak exists.

questions.prompt: Nora says John's Maui habit report proves the morning cue is the whole reason the habit worked. Which reply best fits the source?
choices: The report ties the Maui habit to celebration being key, so the feeling after the act matters.
The report shows the Maui habit works mainly because mornings give people a steady prompt.
The report makes the Maui habit a placeholder that can be replaced by any starter phrase.
questions.explanation: John's report names celebration as key. Reading the case as only a morning prompt misses the source's emotional habit piece.

questions.prompt: "Every habit system already treats celebration as central," Alice says after hearing Deborah D.'s story. What should change in that reading?
choices: Deborah D. was only saying older systems used the wrong kind of celebration.
Deborah D. said other habit books had not tied habits with celebrations for her.
Deborah D. meant celebration should wait until the habit is already automatic.
questions.explanation: The source contrasts Tiny Habits with prior books for Deborah D. The near miss is assuming everyone already taught this tie.

questions.prompt: Caroline celebrates a small win after the first tiny lunch step, then sees the same step tomorrow. What is the likely pull?
choices: The next step waits for a longer streak before it can feel attractive.
The next step can feel more inviting because the small win was tied to it.
The next step becomes automatic only after the whole lunch habit is stable.
questions.explanation: Deborah D. links small-win celebration with looking forward to doing habits. The feeling can pull the next repeat before a long streak exists.

questions.prompt: Bradley says feeling good has little to do with starting tiny because tiny actions are mostly about size. Which correction fits the success reports?
choices: Feeling good and Shine can belong with starting tiny because relief makes the next step less mountain-sized.
Feeling good belongs only after the full habit is complete because starting tiny is just setup.
Feeling good is mostly a way to describe motivation before the tiny behavior begins.
questions.explanation: A success report links feeling good and Shine with starting tiny. The source does not isolate the feeling from the method's habit mechanism.

questions.prompt: Maurice hears a report pairing working out, feeling Shine, and not missing a day. Which reading does that report support?
choices: Immediate positive feeling can support consistency while the action is being repeated.
Consistency must be proven before positive feeling has any role in the habit.
Working out stays consistent only when the action is large enough to feel serious.
questions.explanation: The report presents Shine alongside continued action. The common error reverses the order and waits for consistency before feeling can help.

questions.prompt: Kathleen keeps the Maui habit but removes the celebration because the prompt is already easy. What does John's report challenge?
choices: It challenges the idea that the Maui habit needs a morning cue at all.
It challenges the idea that starter habits should stay easy enough to repeat.
It challenges the idea that celebration is optional once a starter habit is easy.
questions.explanation: John's report ties the Maui habit to celebration as key. Ease and a cue do not make the emotional piece optional.

questions.prompt: During the farmers market talk, Caroline hears, "Deborah D. just wanted a nicer reward after habits were automatic." Which answer best corrects that reading?
choices: The report says older books used rewards too early, so celebration should be delayed.
The report says the missing part was tying habits with celebrations, not waiting for automaticity.
The report says celebration works only when the habit already has a full streak behind it.
questions.explanation: The source frames celebration as the missing tie, not as a later prize. Joel's reading delays the ingredient Deborah D. says was missing.

questions.prompt: At the farmers market stall, Joel decides to feel proud only after a full week of tiny lunches. What consequence follows from Deborah D.'s report?
choices: The delay makes the tiny lunch more practical because pride will be tied to a proven streak.
The delay protects the habit from false cheer because pride belongs after the outcome.
The delay may weaken the next repeat because the small win is not made attractive now.
questions.explanation: Deborah D. connects small-win celebration with looking forward to habits. Waiting for a streak can remove the feeling that helps tomorrow's repeat.

questions.prompt: Caroline says Shine only matters once a habit is big enough to be impressive. Which reply fits the reported success pattern?
choices: Shine mainly proves that the larger task has finally become worth doing.
Shine belongs outside tiny starts because small actions are not real success yet.
Shine can come from starting tiny because the task no longer feels mountain-sized.
questions.explanation: The report links feeling good and Shine with starting tiny. The wrong reading waits for a large action before allowing the good feeling.

reviewCards.front: How does celebration help a tiny behavior become a habit?
reviewCards.back: Celebration creates a small positive feeling right after the behavior. That feeling makes the action more welcome the next time the cue appears.

reviewCards.front: Why is a performed cheer not enough?
reviewCards.back: The method needs a felt success, not a staged sound. If the celebration feels fake, shrink the behavior or choose a quieter response that feels true.

reviewCards.front: What does John's Maui habit report add to the method?
reviewCards.back: It ties the easy Maui habit to celebration being key. The habit is not just a morning cue; it is a small act followed by a good feeling.

reviewCards.front: What was Deborah D.'s missing habit ingredient?
reviewCards.back: She said other habit books had not tied habits with celebrations for her. The missing piece was the emotional win beside the behavior.

reviewCards.front: Recall Motivation matching (Ch 2): name one concrete moment from these scenes where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Kathleen's renewal note fits. She uses today's concern about money to open the account page, then celebrates that tiny action before the later savings arrives.

reviewCards.front: What are the three parts of the Tiny Habits Recipe?
reviewCards.back: The three parts are Anchor, Behavior, and Celebration. The last part is not extra; it places a felt success right after the tiny action.

implementationPlan.title: Place the True Win
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice putting a real positive feeling beside the tiny behavior. Use Place the True Win: finish the action, pause long enough to feel success, and choose a quieter celebration if the first one feels fake. The win should happen before the next task pulls you away.

ifThenPlans.context: When you finish a tiny action and rush toward the next task.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you rush away, then Place the True Win by stopping for one breath and naming what was actually done.

ifThenPlans.context: When your celebration sounds false in your own ears.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the cheer feels fake, then Place the True Win at a smaller size. Use a nod, a smile, or a quiet yes you can believe.

ifThenPlans.context: When you want to wait for a full streak before feeling proud.
ifThenPlans.plan: If pride keeps moving to the future, then Place the True Win after today's tiny step and let that small win count.

ifThenPlans.context: When an easy starter habit still feels dull.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the action is easy but flat, then Place the True Win right after it. Keep the cue and add the feeling John named as key.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During the next day, after routines you already do, count tiny actions that get a real positive feeling within a breath. Tally real, fake, or skipped.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, change one setup: place a small "felt win?" note where your tiny habit ends. Watch whether that spot gets more real celebrations.

memorableLines.text: Feeling wires what repetition repeats.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the mechanism into six plain words.

memorableLines.text: Celebration has to land.
memorableLines.why: It names the authenticity test without adding jargon.

memorableLines.text: A fake victory teaches nothing.
memorableLines.why: It makes the overcorrection easy to remember.

chapters.title: Growing Your Habits from Tiny to Transformative
chapters.hook: I used to turn one pushup into a full routine. What if growth waits until tiny feels easy?
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like stopping at the smallest version is actually how growth gets a foothold. Keep the tiny act easy, and it can stretch, multiply, or stay useful without shame.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a tiny habit feels ready to grow, mark a visible surface with "easy?" and note two options: stretch or stabilize.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Let a tiny habit grow only after it feels easy and good in real life. It may stretch, multiply, or stabilize; all three count when they keep working.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatrice finishes one wall pushup and reaches for the full workout sheet. That is the common move: the tiny action works once, so you ask it to become the new you by tomorrow. The plan sounds brave. By bedtime it feels heavy, and the one pushup starts to feel like a failed workout.

Forced growth breaks the tiny root. Grow only after the small behavior feels easy and good. A tiny habit can Stretch, Multiply, or Stabilize. It may become a longer practice, seed related habits, or stay tiny because it still helps.

A tiny win earns its next inch. You do not owe every small habit a dramatic future. You listen for the signal: ease, repeat, and a felt yes after the action. Then you choose the next small growth, if any.
breakdown.deepRead:
Growth works when success arrives before pressure. Josef's report makes that plain. He practices 30 tiny habits, yet the smallness has not been thrown away. He celebrates every habit and every small success. The number grew, but the wiring move stayed attached.

Think of growth as three paths. Stretch means one habit gets longer or richer, the way DT reports daily meditation growing past an hour a day. Multiply means one reliable recipe leads to another, as Josef's 30 habits show. DT's wider list also names ketogenic diet and daily coding practice. Stabilize means the habit stays small and keeps doing its quiet job. Small can be finished, not failed.

The official materials support that kind of growth without turning it into guesswork. The 5 new videos can walk you through the method again. The list of 60 habits gives stress, focus, and sleep examples when you are ready to add another recipe. The Cheat Sheet keeps the next design fast instead of making each new habit a long planning project.

Use those tools only after the root is alive. If the original habit still feels awkward, do not pile on a bigger version to prove you care. Keep the action tiny. Keep the prompt clear. Keep the celebration real. Growth should feel like the next small inch, not a punishment for having succeeded once.
breakdown.fullRead:
Nash has a tiny habit that has stayed tiny for months: one line in a notebook after he opens his laptop. It does not become a full journal. It does not become a new identity story. It does one useful job. It gets his mind onto the page before messages pull him away.

That case matters because ambition can bully a working habit. You may think every tiny act needs to become impressive. If one line helps, you ask for a page. If one pushup happens, you ask for a workout. If one breath calms you, you try to own the whole morning. Soon the tiny habit is no longer a root. It is a witness against you.

The better test is not size. The better test is signal. Does the behavior happen without a fight? Does it still fit the prompt? Do you feel even a small yes afterward? If so, you can choose a path. Stretch the habit by one inch. Multiply by adding a related recipe. Stabilize by letting the small version keep working.

DT shows the stretch path without making it a demand. Daily meditation grows to more than an hour each day. The same success report names ketogenic diet adherence, daily journaling, daily coding, and more. That is not a promise that every reader will copy the list. It is proof that small wins can spread across more than one part of life.

Jean B.'s report points to another kind of growth. After a week of tiny successes, confidence and capability grow. That order is easy to miss. You do not have to fix your identity first and then act. You can do small actions, feel them land, and let confidence catch up with your evidence.

The official aids belong on the same side of that test. The 5 new videos can refresh the method. The 60 habits can give you options for tense days, scattered attention, and poor rest. The Cheat Sheet can speed the next recipe. None of those tools means do more today. They help when a tiny success is ready for a next move.

A surface mark can help you hear the signal. Put the word easy on a sticky note, a margin, or your phone wallpaper. When a tiny habit feels steady, write two choices under it: grow one inch or keep it tiny. The mark slows the urge to turn success into pressure.

If the mark does not feel true, do not argue with it. Keep the habit small. Move the prompt closer. Make the action easier. Celebrate the finish with more care. Those repairs may feel plain, but they protect the root that later growth needs.

The precondition is plain: the tiny behavior must already feel easy and a bit good. When that is absent, growth does not need more force. Go back to the original recipe: make it easier, place the prompt, and celebrate the small win.

examples.title: Back Row Sixty
examples.scenario: "Sixty sounds like homework," Beatrice hears from the back row, and the adult class pauses over official materials. She is teaching with 5 new videos listed on the screen and 60 habits sorted for stress, focus, and sleep. The learner's confusion is useful: are the examples a demand, or a shelf to choose from after one tiny recipe works?
examples.whatToDo: Beatrice asks the learner to compare two next cards: leave the current habit stable or add one related recipe. She keeps the list as a shelf, not a race.
examples.whyItMatters: The 60 examples can support growth without forcing it. A class that starts with one working recipe protects ease before it multiplies habits.

examples.title: Thirty Without Force
examples.scenario: "Thirty habits would ruin my day," learner Emmett says on the back porch step, marker uncapped over his Sunday habit card, then sees Josef's success note about 30 tiny habits. Earlier, Emmett stacked new actions into one morning and quit by lunch. Later, with one variable changed, he keeps each action tiny and celebrates every small success. The number no longer acts like a dare.
examples.whatToDo: Emmett rebuilds the list around tiny actions and celebration after each one. He lets the count grow only while the pieces stay easy enough to do.
examples.whyItMatters: Josef's report is not a license to force a crowded routine. It shows multiplication can keep the same tiny recipe and emotional spark.

examples.title: Clean Sheet Crowded List
examples.scenario: The 5 new videos are queued; Claire's 60 habits list is crowded, and Oscar can see both on the coworking lounge table. "Use the Cheat Sheet," he says. "For all 60 habits?" Claire asks. "For the next one." "And the rest?" "Park them." "So the tool is for adding one good recipe, not proving I can carry 60 habits?" Oscar nods.
examples.whatToDo: Oscar keeps the talk on one next recipe. He uses the Cheat Sheet to make the next design fast, then leaves the rest of Claire's list alone.
examples.whyItMatters: A fast tool can still be misused slowly. The Cheat Sheet helps growth when it speeds one clean addition, not when it hides a pile of pressure.

examples.title: Mentor Seat Pause
examples.scenario: The practice host drops Pauline into the mentor seat, although she came to watch. DT's list is on the screen: daily meditation over an hour, ketogenic diet, daily journaling, daily coding. Her first thought is wrong: I should tell everyone to aim there. Her second thought slows down. DT did not start with a mountain. The growth came after small wins could carry more.
examples.whatToDo: Pauline writes one private note before she speaks: name the current tiny win first. Then she frames DT's domains as possible spread, not the starting line.
examples.whyItMatters: A big success report can tempt you to copy the end state. Organic habit growth asks what tiny behavior is already reliable enough to carry more.

examples.title: One Hour Allocation
examples.scenario: Planner Aline drags the focus row above stress behind the hotel front desk during the workshop prep hour, with 5 new videos beside the list of 60 habits. The one file she meant to save is gone from the desk computer, and her attention is thin. The choice is not between success and failure. Her hour can buy one clean recipe, one Cheat Sheet pass, or a tour of every idea.
examples.whatToDo: Aline protects the scarce hour. She compares one easy recipe with one wider tour, then spends the planning slot on the recipe most likely to start.
examples.whyItMatters: Growth can fail before action begins. When attention is scarce, choosing one next recipe beats sampling every official example.

examples.title: Scrapped Grid Cost
examples.scenario: The folder clasp sticks halfway, and Nash's thumb catches on the packet rings in a courthouse hallway habit workshop. His printed grid turns 5 new videos and 60 habits into one rushed expansion plan. Two bad choices sit there. Nash must choose while people line up: hand out a plan that may push unwired habits too hard, or scrap the polished grid and waste the packets he paid for. He drops the grid in recycling before anyone sees a payoff.
examples.whatToDo: Nash keeps one blank Cheat Sheet and writes one line at the top: grow only after easy. He takes the awkward cost before the room rewards the simpler handout.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost is paid first. Organic growth often starts by giving up the impressive plan before the smaller design has proved itself.

questions.prompt: "I'll remember how to add new habits once life slows down," Pauline says after seeing the official page list 5 new videos. What does her answer miss?
choices: She should choose a larger habit first so memory has a stronger target.
She should wait for free time before using any design help.
She has step-by-step video support instead of relying on memory.
questions.explanation: The 5 videos are design support. Pauline is treating growth as something memory must hold alone, while the source gives guided help.

questions.prompt: Aline thinks Tiny Habits gives only one starter move, so she stops after the first recipe. Which detail should change her plan?
choices: The first recipe should become larger before she adds any new area.
The official examples include 60 habits across stress, focus, and sleep.
The sleep example should replace stress and focus until it works.
questions.explanation: The source lists 60 habit designs for several life areas. Aline is missing the range of examples and reading the method as one starter only.

questions.prompt: "I need a long planning session before each new habit," Claire says while holding the Cheat Sheet. Which reply fits the source?
choices: The Cheat Sheet is meant to make new recipe design fast.
The Cheat Sheet works only after a full habit review.
The Cheat Sheet should make each plan more formal.
questions.explanation: The source names a Cheat Sheet for creating habits fast. Claire's long-session reading misses the tool's role in keeping growth simple.

questions.prompt: Emmett sees Josef's report of 30 tiny habits and says, "Tiny must mean one behavior only." What does the report show instead?
choices: The count works only if the habits stop being tiny.
The report is mainly about replacing the first recipe.
The method can multiply beyond one tiny recipe.
questions.explanation: Josef reports 30 tiny habits. The source supports multiplication, not the idea that tiny allows only one behavior.

questions.prompt: Josef celebrates every habit and every small success, but Nash wants to drop celebration once his list grows. Which response matches the report?
choices: Nash should keep celebration attached as habits multiply.
Nash should save celebration for the largest habit only.
Nash should use celebration only while learning the first habit.
questions.explanation: Josef keeps celebration with every habit and small success. Dropping it after multiplication removes the emotional wiring that the report preserves.

questions.prompt: DT reports meditation growing to over an hour a day. Claire says tiny habits can only stay symbolic. Which reading is better?
choices: The report makes tiny starts useful only for short calming breaks.
The report shows a tiny start can stretch into a substantial practice.
The report proves meditation should grow before other habits do.
questions.explanation: DT's meditation report gives a clear stretch case. It shows that a tiny start can become substantial without making growth mandatory for every habit.

questions.prompt: DT also names ketogenic diet, journaling, coding, and more. Aline says the method is just for health habits. What should she revise?
choices: She should limit coding to a reward after health habits are set.
She should move journaling and diet outside habit design.
She should see growth spreading across several life areas.
questions.explanation: The source names diet, journaling, coding, and more. DT's report is broader than health alone, so Aline should revise that narrow reading.

questions.prompt: After one week of tiny successes, Jean B. reports more confidence and capability. Aline says she must feel capable before small habits can work. Which reading fits the timing?
choices: Confidence can grow from repeated small actions before identity feels fixed.
Confidence should be declared first so small actions feel natural.
Confidence matters only after a large outside result appears.
questions.explanation: Jean B. ties confidence to tiny successes over a week. The source points to identity change following action, not needing to arrive first.

questions.prompt: Oscar's habit list grows, and he says, "Celebration was for the starter phase." Which practice would keep the growth source-faithful?
choices: He should replace celebration with a weekly count once the list grows.
He should celebrate each habit and each small success as the list grows.
He should reserve celebration for habits that become large enough.
questions.explanation: The Josef report keeps celebration attached to every habit and small success. Oscar's starter-phase reading cuts off a core support too early.

reviewCards.front: What signal should come before a tiny habit grows?
reviewCards.back: The original behavior should feel easy, repeatable, and a little good. Growth follows that signal; it does not replace the tiny behavior before it is wired.

reviewCards.front: How do Stretch, Multiply, and Stabilize differ?
reviewCards.back: Stretch makes one habit larger, Multiply adds related tiny recipes, and Stabilize keeps the small version working. All three can be valid growth paths.

reviewCards.front: What does Josef's 30-habit report teach about multiplication?
reviewCards.back: Multiplication can keep the tiny method intact. Josef reports 30 tiny habits while still celebrating every habit and every small success.

reviewCards.front: Why does DT's report matter for organic habit growth?
reviewCards.back: DT shows spread across several domains: meditation, diet, journaling, coding, and more. The lesson is spillover after reliable wins, not a demand to copy every domain.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more here: emotion as habit wiring (Ch 5) or organic habit growth, and why?
reviewCards.back: Organic habit growth is the main idea because the situation asks when to stretch, multiply, or stabilize. Emotion still matters because celebration helps the tiny win feel safe enough to grow.

reviewCards.front: How do the videos, the 60 habits, and the Cheat Sheet help without forcing growth?
reviewCards.back: They give support when a tiny behavior is ready: video help, many examples, and a fast design aid. The tools serve the signal; they do not create pressure by themselves.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Growth Signal
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice hearing when a tiny habit is ready for more. Mark the Growth Signal by asking whether the action feels easy, repeatable, and good after you do it. Then choose Stretch, Multiply, or Stabilize instead of pushing every habit to become big.

ifThenPlans.context: When one tiny habit works and you want to make it bigger right away.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the urge to grow shows up, then Mark the Growth Signal first. Ask whether the tiny version is easy and good before you add size.

ifThenPlans.context: When you want a list of new habits after one success.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list starts growing, then Mark the Growth Signal for one current habit. Multiply only while each small success still gets celebrated.

ifThenPlans.context: When a tiny practice feels steady and asks for a little more time.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the habit feels ready to stretch, then Mark the Growth Signal and add one small inch, not the full future version.

ifThenPlans.context: When a tiny habit stays tiny but keeps helping.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the small version still works, then Mark the Growth Signal as Stabilize. Let useful smallness count as success.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a tiny habit feels easy, mark a surface you already see with "EASY." Under it, write two choices: grow one inch or keep it tiny.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of the week, look back once at your marked surface and name what changed about your growth signal: Stretch, Multiply, or Stabilize. Do not keep a daily log.

memorableLines.text: Forced growth breaks the tiny root.
memorableLines.why: It gives the hard edge a short warning the reader can use before over-scaling.

memorableLines.text: A tiny win earns its next inch.
memorableLines.why: It makes growth conditional on earned ease instead of pressure.

memorableLines.text: Small can be finished, not failed.
memorableLines.why: It makes Stabilize feel like a valid path, not a consolation prize.

chapters.title: Untangling Bad Habits: A Systematic Solution
chapters.hook: The spotless vow slid under the snack bowl, and the snack bowl kept winning.
chapters.counterintuition: A bad habit can feel personal and still be a design problem. The act is not excused; the repair starts with the link you can change.
chapters.tryThisNow: For the next ten minutes, before you send your next reply, pre-write the words you'll use after a slip: "What prompt fired, and what link can I change?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a bad habit repeats, map its prompt, ease, and pull; change the easiest link first, and leave shame out so repair stays possible.

breakdown.fastRead:
Emilia peels the cleanup chart off the cabinet while Blake holds the marker. They are equal roommates, so neither wins by rank. Blake thinks a stricter chart will fix the snack pile. Emilia thinks the chart is more clutter. Candace P.'s report gives her the test: stop adding willpower and discipline, then work with a few key variables. Blake yields. They move the snack bowl, delete the delivery shortcut, and keep one visible water glass.

Bad habits obey design, not drama. B=MAP still applies: the behavior needs Motivation, Ability, and Prompt. Start with the easiest link. Remove the cue before you wrestle the craving.
breakdown.deepRead:
Annabelle's missed session is already a joke in the group chat. Her coach asks, "Back tomorrow?" Annabelle types, "I blew it. Typical." Then the coach sends Brad's line back to her: change can happen without negative self talk, even when motivation is low or a session is missed. Annabelle deletes the verdict and writes one restart sentence.

The system is simple. An unwanted action still asks for three things: pull, ease, and cue. Motivation is the pull. Ability is how easy the act feels. Prompt is the cue that says now. If one link gets weaker, the behavior becomes less likely.

Use the Bad-Habit Levers in order: Remove prompt, Reduce ability, Redirect motivation. Remove prompt means move the cue before it fires. Put the snack bowl in a cabinet. Park the phone in the hall. Reduce ability means make the unwanted act harder. Add a step, distance, or pause. Redirect motivation means feed a better pull, such as relief, care, or one tiny replacement.

Shame makes a poor repair tool. It can feel like proof that you care, but it often pushes you out of the process. Brad's case is the warning. Low motivation and a missed session call for a design change small enough to try.
breakdown.fullRead:
The streak did not end on the hard day. It ended in the three texts after it. In Yvonne's postmortem, the evidence is small: low motivation, one missed session, then negative self talk, then a skipped restart. Brad's report names the hinge. The missed session survived. The judgment after it turned one miss into a week away.

PM's all-or-nothing pattern starts clean and ends empty. The standard was total success or nothing, and the result was nothing. You know this shape. You promise no scrolling, no snacks, no missed workouts, no late replies. The promise sounds clean. The first slip then feels like the whole plan is broken.

Your notebook needs a camera-level line first. Do not write "be better at night." Write "open the shopping app in bed" or "eat from the bowl beside the couch." Behavior is something a camera could see. A plain behavior gives you something to redesign.

A phone alert can be the first link. So can walking through the kitchen after work. If the cue is visible, remove it or move it. If the cue is a routine, change the path. Put the keys in a different bowl. Charge the phone outside the room.

The app stays signed in until you make the old act harder. This does not mean punish yourself. It means add enough friction that the old act no longer wins by being easy. Sign out of the app. Buy the snack in a smaller package. Put the card in a drawer. Ability works both ways. If ease helps a wanted habit, friction can slow an unwanted one.

The pull may be stress relief, boredom, belonging, or fear of missing out. If the pull is real, do not pretend the cue alone explains everything. Add a tiny replacement that gives some honest relief. Text one sentence. Pour water. Step outside for a minute.

Candace's report points to why this stays humane. She moved away from willpower and discipline toward the variables that mattered. Fewer variables mean less clutter in the repair. You do not need a court case against yourself. You need the link that gives way first.

Blake and Emilia show the social side of the repair. Blake sees the old habit and wants a stronger rule. Emilia sees the same habit and wants the easier link. Both care about the shared home. The useful turn is not that Emilia wins. It is that Blake yields when the evidence points to prompt and ease. Good redesign can change a mind without shaming the person who changed it.

Rent due tonight is not a tiny-design puzzle. If the account is short, moving a shopping app off the front screen will not cover the payment. Call the landlord, ask for help, change the money flow, or cancel the charge now. If a behavior involves addiction, danger, or medical risk, get trained support. Behavior design can weaken a chain. It cannot replace protection, treatment, or money that is already due.

examples.title: Chart Comes Down
examples.scenario: Emilia pinches the cleanout chart halfway off the living-room cabinet after dinner while Blake, her equal roommate, keeps his marker uncapped. He predicts the stricter chart will beat another messy week. Emilia predicts the opposite after Candace P.'s shift from willpower and discipline to a few key variables. The reveal comes when Blake yields first: the chart comes down, the snack bowl moves, and the shopping shortcut leaves the front screen.
examples.whatToDo: Emilia asks Blake to test one variable before adding another rule. She removes the prompt and makes the unwanted snack run less easy.
examples.whyItMatters: Candace P.'s case turns a willpower fight into a design test. The repair gets smaller, and the person stops being the problem.

examples.title: Group Chat Restart
examples.scenario: Annabelle's missed session had already become a joke on her phone screen at the gym bench, and the new runner sees it above her towel after class. Coach: "Back tomorrow?" Annabelle: "I blew it. Typical." Coach: "Brad says change can happen without negative self talk, even when motivation is low." Annabelle: "So I write the next tiny start, not a verdict?" Coach: "Yes. One line."
examples.whatToDo: Annabelle deletes the self-attack and writes the restart line. She keeps the miss in the process instead of letting judgment end it.
examples.whyItMatters: A text thread can pull you toward shame fast. Brad's case shows why the next design move matters more than the harsher verdict.

examples.title: Counter Reset
examples.scenario: Jenna is restacking every supplement bottle on the pharmacy counter when the clerk calls the next pickup and breaks her all-or-nothing spell. PM's phrase, all or nothing produced nothing, finally names the pattern. She closes the big tracker, stops, and restarts: one bottle goes beside the toothbrush, and the rest stay in the bag.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna stops the total reset and places one prompt where the first dose can start. The rest of the plan waits until the first link works.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is the repair. PM's case warns that a complete restart can become another way to get nothing done.

examples.title: Desk With Fewer Rules
examples.scenario: Henry's lunch break is thinning while the clerk works at the clinic reception desk: sticky notes for no soda, a budget card, a habit app badge, a half-filled water bottle. None is wrong, but the pile feels like another chore. Candace P.'s report points away from willpower clutter and toward a few key variables. Henry moves the soda coupon out of sight and leaves the water where his hand lands.
examples.whatToDo: Henry removes one visible cue and leaves one easy replacement in the path. He clears the desk enough for the better action to show up.
examples.whyItMatters: A small desk can hold too many rules. Candace P.'s case makes the fix simpler: fewer variables, less willpower talk, one changed cue.

examples.title: Voice Memo Aftermath
examples.scenario: The voice memo on the living-room couch is short, and the week after the skipped class is gone. Yvonne is a new runner reviewing her own missed session. Her notes do not make the miss the villain. Low motivation made the start easy to skip, then the message on her phone made it sound final: "I always quit." Brad's report gives the cleaner read. Change can happen without negative self talk and judgment. The miss needed a tiny restart; the judgment talked her out of it.
examples.whatToDo: Yvonne marks the self-attack as the link to change. She drafts the next restart line before she reviews the missed session again.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem shows how one miss can survive when judgment does not get the last word. Brad's case keeps the repair small and non-shaming.

examples.title: Vow Crossed Out
examples.scenario: "You made it too perfect," someone says from the next locker, and Ella stops writing her no-scroll vow on the gym bench. She has copied PM's failed all-or-nothing shape without meaning to: total ban, no slip plan, nothing after one miss. The noticing stings. She crosses out the vow and writes one friction change instead: the app leaves the home screen before bed.
examples.whatToDo: Ella corrects the mistake while the vow is still wet. She reduces ability for the unwanted scroll instead of betting on total force.
examples.whyItMatters: Mistake recovery begins when you catch your own pattern. PM's case shows why a friction change can beat another perfect ban.

questions.prompt: During a late-night phone cleanup, Blake says, "If it is a bad habit, B=MAP no longer applies." Which reply fits the model?
choices: He should treat the late scroll as a willpower lapse and renew the same vow tomorrow.
He should map Motivation, Ability, and Prompt because unwanted actions still need all three.
He should skip the model and look only for a stronger reason to care about sleep.
questions.explanation: B=MAP applies to any behavior. The scroll is not outside design; it still needs pull, ease, and a cue that can be changed.

questions.prompt: Ella keeps grabbing candy after walking through the lobby and says, "The craving starts inside me." What is she missing?
choices: The craving may need a stronger reason before the lobby habit can change.
The craving may prove the candy habit is too personal for prompt work.
The lobby walk may be the routine prompt that starts the chain.
questions.explanation: Prompts can be routine-based, not only internal urges. Changing the path or cue can interrupt the chain before the craving gets louder.

questions.prompt: Jenna signs out of a shopping app and removes the saved card while her phone charges across the room. What effect is she aiming for?
choices: She is trying to raise motivation by making the purchase feel more serious.
She is trying to make friction useful only after a replacement habit is stable.
She is trying to lower ability for the unwanted action by adding steps.
questions.explanation: Making the unwanted behavior harder lowers ability. The extra steps reduce the chance that the old action wins by being easy.

questions.prompt: "Candace P. proves we need stronger discipline," Henry says while adding another rule card. Which reading fits her report?
choices: Her report shows discipline should stay central until the rule cards finally work.
Her report shows willpower is useful only when the habit is already automatic.
Her report moves from willpower and discipline toward a few key variables.
questions.explanation: Candace P. contrasts willpower and discipline with a few variables. More rule cards repeat the error her report helps correct.

questions.prompt: Annabelle adds several new tracking sheets to the counter after a snack habit slips again. Which result should she watch for?
choices: The extra rules may add clutter when fewer variables would make repair clearer.
The extra rules may work once she pairs each sheet with a harsher consequence.
The extra rules may prove the habit needs discipline before any prompt changes.
questions.explanation: Candace P.'s report values clearing clutter and focusing on fewer variables. Adding sheets can hide the prompt or ease problem.

questions.prompt: "I missed again, so I should talk to myself harder," Yvonne says after a skipped session. What does Brad's case suggest?
choices: She should keep the hard self-talk brief so the next session still feels possible.
She should remove judgment because shame can push her out of the process.
She should save the judgment for later because low motivation needs a delayed review.
questions.explanation: Brad links change with less negative self talk and judgment. The repair should keep Yvonne engaged, not make the miss a verdict.

questions.prompt: A low-motivation week leaves Blake with one missed workout and a packed bag by the door. Which next reading keeps the repair open?
choices: A missed session can survive, so he should design the next tiny restart.
A missed session means the method failed, so he should wait for higher drive.
A missed session should trigger a larger plan to prove he still cares.
questions.explanation: Brad mentions low motivation and missed sessions without treating them as fatal. The next move is recovery, not proof that the design is dead.

questions.prompt: Emilia writes a no-snacks plan on the fridge and says, "This time I will quit perfectly or not bother." What does PM's report warn is likely?
choices: The perfect standard may feel cleaner once the first prompt has been removed.
The all-or-nothing frame may collapse into nothing after the first slip.
The larger vow may help if she adds enough tracking to support it.
questions.explanation: PM names all-or-nothing as the pattern that led to nothing. The oversized standard makes one slip feel like total failure.

questions.prompt: Henry wants to replace late-night scrolling with a long workout plan that starts when he is already tired. Which risk comes first?
choices: The replacement is too complicated, so the old habit may stay easier.
The replacement is too small, so it may not feel important enough to count.
The replacement is too clear, so the prompt may lose its social pressure.
questions.explanation: A complicated replacement adds friction. The prompt should ask for a tiny alternative, or the unwanted behavior may remain the easier path.

reviewCards.front: How does B=MAP help when the behavior is unwanted?
reviewCards.back: It keeps the bad habit inside the same model. The unwanted action still needs Motivation, Ability, and Prompt, so you can find which link to weaken.

reviewCards.front: What are the three Bad-Habit Levers, and what does each change?
reviewCards.back: They are Remove prompt, Reduce ability, and Redirect motivation. Remove the cue, make the unwanted action harder, or shift the pull toward a tiny better act.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate prompt as the now signal (Ch 4), then use it on an unwanted habit?
reviewCards.back: A prompt is the cue that says start now. For a bad habit, use that idea backward: find the cue that starts the unwanted action, then move, hide, or replace it.

reviewCards.front: Why does Candace P.'s case push against willpower clutter?
reviewCards.back: Her report moves away from willpower and discipline toward a few key variables. That means the repair should get clearer, not heavier with rules.

reviewCards.front: Why is negative self talk a weak repair after a miss?
reviewCards.back: It can turn one missed session into a reason to quit. Brad's case shows that low motivation and a miss need a restart design, not judgment.

reviewCards.front: How does PM's all-or-nothing report warn you about oversized standards?
reviewCards.back: PM describes all or nothing leading to nothing. A total vow can make one slip feel final, so the safer repair is a smaller link change.

implementationPlan.title: Break the Easiest Link
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice finding the weakest point in an unwanted behavior chain. Break the Easiest Link by naming the prompt, ease, or pull that keeps the habit alive. Change that link before you write a bigger vow.

ifThenPlans.context: When the unwanted action starts after the same place, object, or routine.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the cue repeats, then Break the Easiest Link by moving the object or changing the path before the old action fires.

ifThenPlans.context: When the bad habit wins because it is the easiest act in the room.
ifThenPlans.plan: If ease is feeding it, then Break the Easiest Link by adding one step between you and the unwanted action.

ifThenPlans.context: When self-criticism starts right after a missed session.
ifThenPlans.plan: If judgment starts, then Break the Easiest Link by writing one restart sentence before the self-attack gets rehearsed.

ifThenPlans.context: When your new rule sounds total, perfect, or all-or-nothing.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the vow sounds perfect, then Break the Easiest Link by crossing out the vow and changing one prompt or friction point.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, before you send one response about a habit you keep missing, pre-write this reply: "I am changing the prompt first." Add one next tiny step.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time the unwanted behavior starts after the same prompt. At week's end, read the number and change the cue with the highest tally.

memorableLines.text: Bad habits obey design, not drama.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the anti-shame repair into one plain contrast.

memorableLines.text: Remove the cue before you wrestle the craving.
memorableLines.why: It makes prompt removal feel like the first practical move.

memorableLines.text: Shame makes a poor repair tool.
memorableLines.why: It gives Brad's non-shaming lesson a short, memorable form.

chapters.title: How We Change Together
chapters.hook: Could one warm sentence after a tiny win do more than another reminder?
chapters.counterintuition: Despite how helpful advice can feel in your mouth, pressure makes the habit heavier. A small cue and a fast celebration often help more than another lecture.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to remind someone again, move one cue beside a thing they touch and swap the reminder for "Try the tiny ask."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Help changes people when it makes the next tiny action easier to start, easier to remember, and worth celebrating right away, without turning support into pressure.

breakdown.fastRead:
Blair has one line left in a reply. The participant wrote, "I missed it again," and Blair can feel the lecture forming. She deletes it. She writes back with a smaller recipe and one sentence of praise for noticing the miss.

Pressure makes help heavier. When you support a habit, your job is not to make the other person feel watched. Your job is to make the next tiny action easier to do and easier to notice.

Celebrate the step, not the performance. A win can be as small as replying, trying once, or moving the cue into sight. If the other person feels success, the next repeat has a place to stand.
breakdown.deepRead:
A one-line reply can do more than a long lecture. In the 5-Day Program, automated daily check-in emails can handle the routine nudge, while a human coach gives personalized feedback and email guidance. That split is smart. The routine nudge can stay plain every time. The human part is saved for the moment when a person needs help shaping the recipe.

Social behavior design means helping a behavior happen with another person in the loop. It still begins with the smallest useful act. The shared recipe has three parts: Shrink the ask, Anchor the prompt, Celebrate the win. Shrink the ask so the other person can start. Anchor the prompt so the cue is tied to a real moment. Celebrate the win so success feels seen right away.

Bailey gets this wrong at first. When a participant misses two check-ins, Bailey wants to raise the standard. Make the habit bigger. Ask for proof. Send a firmer note. Blair points to the shorter path: make the next recipe clearer, not heavier. If the person meant to drink water after brushing teeth, the coach might ask for a single sip when the toothbrush is put down. Then the reply can praise the sip.

A tiny win shared well can travel. James Clear is listed as signing up for the program in 2012, and that case reports a changed life and career. That does not mean one signup guarantees a career. It means a small method can move through a person who later teaches many others. The social chain begins with one act made easy enough to repeat.
breakdown.fullRead:
Thierry wants to send the paragraph. It is careful, kind, and much too long. The person on the other end has already missed the habit and may be one more note away from quitting. Thierry trims the reply until it asks for one small action and names one thing already done well.

That trim is the price of useful help. You give up the pleasure of sounding wise. You give up the rush of fixing the whole problem in one message. You give up the big speech that proves you care. In return, the other person gets a next step they can actually take.

The 5-Day Program shows the split. The auto check-ins can carry the routine part. A human coach can use email guidance for personalized feedback, answers, and guidance. The coach does not need to prove closeness by typing every prompt. The coach adds value where the recipe needs shaping.

Think of support as size, cue, and celebration. If any part grows too large, support starts to feel like supervision. A smaller ask says, "You can begin here." A real prompt says, "You will know when to begin." A fast celebration says, "That counted."

James Clear's 2012 case is the cleanest cascade. One signup is a small act. The public page says the program changed his life and career. Later readers met habit ideas through his wider work. You do not need to overstate the link to learn from it. A tiny design can travel farther when a person carries it into new rooms.

Mark's family case keeps the same idea close to home. After finishing the program, he taught the behavior model to his two daughters, including a 17 year old. The useful part is not a parent winning an argument. The useful part is shared language. A household can stop saying, "Try harder," and start asking, "What would make the next step easier?"

You will feel the cost when you help someone you love. They miss the walk, the pill, the text, the budget check. Your first urge may be to remind them again, louder this time. The tiny-ask move asks you to do less in public and more in design. Move the cue. Lower the action. Praise the attempt. None of this gives you the control a lecture seems to offer.

That lost control is real. Some moments need a clear demand, especially when safety, money, or trust is at risk. If a bill is due today, a tiny ask is not a substitute for paying it. If a promise affects someone else, warmth cannot erase the repair owed. Social behavior design helps with repeat actions, not urgent harm.

Blair sees the cost at the end of the reply. Her longer note would have named every pattern. Her shorter note only says, "Try one sip after the brush goes down. Nice job noticing the miss." She sends it and lets the rest wait. The help becomes smaller than her wisdom, so the habit can become larger than her advice.

examples.title: Two Coach Replies
examples.scenario: Blair's two-line reply sits above Bailey's full lecture in the human coach inbox, and both answer the same automated daily check-in email. Blair sends personalized feedback that shrinks the next sip after brushing. Bailey writes a warmer but heavier note asking for a full reset. One participant replies with a tiny win. The other lets the message sink under the day's mental clutter.
examples.whatToDo: Blair keeps the human part focused on recipe feedback. She names the next tiny action and celebrates the reply instead of adding pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: Two kind messages can land in opposite ways. Social support helps when it makes success easier to reach, not when it makes failure louder.

examples.title: Clipboard By Email
examples.scenario: The senior coach's reply queue lands in Hunter's inbox while automated daily check-in emails keep arriving on their own. He thought a human coach had to type the daily nudge. Thierry points to personalized feedback instead. "Your job is not to push the habit. Your job is to make success easier to see." Hunter changes the next answer from a pep talk to one clear tweak.
examples.whatToDo: Hunter answers the recipe, not the person's character. He sends one adjustment and one clear celebration for reporting the miss.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe saves the human coach for the work automation cannot do. A person can notice confusion and make the next action feel possible.

examples.title: Seventeen At The Table
examples.scenario: 17 is old enough for Allison to hear a lecture coming as father Mark sets a rinsed plate beside her school notebook at the dinner table. He has finished the program and wants to teach his two daughters the behavior model, but Finn hears "try harder" before he starts. Allison asks whether the model means she failed. Mark slows down. The lesson becomes her confusion: what would make the next tiny action easier.
examples.whatToDo: Allison names the fear under the lesson, and Mark changes the talk into a shared question about the next tiny action.
examples.whyItMatters: Family language helps only when it lowers shame. A model shared at home should make the next step easier, not give the household new labels for blame.

examples.title: Sticky Sign-Up
examples.scenario: James Clear's trackpad sticks on the signup button, and the small act almost feels too ordinary to count. In 2012, the page lists him as a participant, not just a later endorser. The same public case later says the program changed his life and career. One variable changes across the two views: a tiny method is no longer private once a future teacher carries it outward.
examples.whatToDo: James Clear takes the small entry step, then the case lets the later spread remain a cascade rather than a guaranteed formula.
examples.whyItMatters: A small act can open a large path without promising the same path for everyone. Social change spreads through people, not through pressure.

examples.title: Buzz In The Thread
examples.scenario: The phone buzzes against Donovan's palm, and the sound is Allison's automated daily check-in email. Donovan, the human coach, reads, "I missed two days. Should I start over?" He types, "Only if the recipe is too big." Allison: "So not a lecture?" Donovan: "No. One sip after brushing, then count the reply as a win." Allison: "That I can try."
examples.whatToDo: Donovan gives personalized feedback through the email thread. He changes the recipe size and names the reply itself as a win.
examples.whyItMatters: A short exchange can keep support from becoming pressure. The coach helps by changing the recipe, not by raising the emotional cost.

examples.title: Mug Before Send
examples.scenario: Thierry's mug pauses halfway to the saucer while the draft reply waits. Too soft, he thinks. They missed two days. Maybe the kind thing is to be clear. No, clear is not the same as heavy. The automated daily check-in email already asked. The human coach part is this: personalized feedback, one visible win. He cuts the paragraph down before sending.
examples.whatToDo: Thierry uses the automated check-in as the prompt and saves his human effort for one recipe change and one celebration.
examples.whyItMatters: Inner pressure can disguise itself as care. The useful social move is smaller, clearer, and more likely to be tried.

questions.prompt: "I thought the course was just emails I read alone," Blair says after seeing the sign-up page. What does that response miss?
choices: The program relies on self-study emails with no human support.
The program includes help from a kind and supportive human coach.
The program centers on live group calls before habits begin.

reviewCards.front: What are the three parts of Social Tiny Habit Support?
reviewCards.back: Shrink the ask, Anchor the prompt, and Celebrate the win. Support works when it makes the action smaller, ties it to a real cue, and makes success feel noticed.

reviewCards.front: Why can a human coach matter when daily check-ins are automated?
reviewCards.back: Automation can carry the routine prompt. The coach matters when a person needs personal recipe feedback, answers, and guidance instead of another generic nudge.

reviewCards.front: What does pressure get wrong about helping another person's habit?
reviewCards.back: Pressure tries to raise effort. Social behavior design lowers the next action, improves the prompt, and celebrates the small success so the person can repeat it.

reviewCards.front: What does James Clear's 2012 case show without promising?
reviewCards.back: It shows a tiny method can move outward through someone who later teaches many others. It does not promise every signup will change a career.

reviewCards.front: How would motivation matching (Ch 2) change the way you help someone with a tiny ask?
reviewCards.back: It would size the social ask to the drive present now. If the other person is tired, make the help lighter: easier action, clearer prompt, quick celebration.

implementationPlan.title: Swap in the Tiny Ask
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice replacing pressure with a tiny ask. When you want to remind, correct, or motivate someone, shrink the action first. Then place the cue near a thing they already touch and celebrate the next small success.

ifThenPlans.context: You feel the pull to remind someone again.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you feel the pull to remind someone again, then Swap in the Tiny Ask: name one smaller action and move one cue near a thing they already touch.

ifThenPlans.context: A person reports a miss in a check-in, text, or reply.
ifThenPlans.plan: If someone reports a miss, then Swap in the Tiny Ask by changing the recipe before you comment on effort.

ifThenPlans.context: A group wants to make the habit bigger because morale feels high.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the group wants a bigger target, then Swap in the Tiny Ask and keep only the action that can be prompted and celebrated today.

ifThenPlans.context: You want to share a course, tool, or routine with a friend.
ifThenPlans.plan: If sharing starts to feel like fixing, then Swap in the Tiny Ask by offering one small first step and leaving the choice open.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, when you want to push a habit on someone, attach one tiny ask to an object they already touch, then celebrate the smallest yes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For the first half of the week, use one reminder as you normally would. For the second half, replace it with Swap in the Tiny Ask and compare which one gets a calmer yes.
